body: Slower at reading than at writing, the boy is set to copy out each day's psalm or minute a second time, and by the spring his fair copies, stroke for stroke exact, are pinned the length of the byre's one dry wall.

title: The maor visits the byre school and writes nothing
body: The shire's maor, whose office is to note anything newly opened in it, rides out, watches the children recite a psalm, asks Agnes Pike only after the room's heating and the children's fees, and sends south that season a report of harvest, head-due and bridge that says nothing of the school at all.

title: Alice Hale opens a second school at Caol mhòr
body: Walter Hale's daughter Alice opens a school of her own in a disused net-store behind the harbour at Caol mhòr, on a purse thinner than her father carried north, and writes to Agnes Pike asking what has answered best on the byre's cold mornings.

title: The Cill ghlas fault line walked and found unmoved
body: Lachlann mac Iain Bhàin and his chainman Iain mac Ruairidh trace the old Cill ghlas fault foot by foot with plumb and cord and file a report at Cathair mhòr declaring the district safe to work again so long as new shafts are cut a full chain back from it.

title: The school moves to the church porch for summer
body: With the widow's cattle wanting the byre back for the warm months, Agnes Pike's school moves into the porch of the Doire ghlas church, a change it makes every summer after.

title: Daniel Frayne copies the minute of the school's own founding
body: On the last morning before the move to the church porch, Agnes Pike sets her best copyist the Moot's own four-line minute recording the school's opening, and pins his fair copy into the register's first leaf rather than to the drying wall.

title: Eilidh nic Leòid opens the Ceann mhòr assize
body: In the heat of an t-Iuchar, with the windows of the old magistrate's house propped open against the fish-yard smell, Eilidh nic Leòid tells the crowded room that she will hear all nineteen causes on the list to their own ends, in their own order, whatever the likeness of one paper to the next, and whatever the weather asks of everyone waiting on the bench.

title: The Dunlop title read to its end
body: Eilidh nic Leòid reads a human grant brown at its folds, and a receipt for seed corn the family thought to bring unasked, and finds as she found seven years before at Seann Bhral: the ground is the Crown's, the working of it the Dunlops', on the same terms as before and no excusal from any due to come.

title: Fifteen suits found for the Crown at Ceann mhòr
body: Cause after cause of the seventeen brought on human titles is decided in the words of the Leòid ruling, the ground passing to the Crown and the working of it staying with the family that holds it, until the room has learned, before the week is out, to stop guessing at an ending it already knows.

title: A custodian's countersign found on the Coombe title
body: In the margin of a Tuathaich family's human grant, Eilidh nic Leòid finds the pressed mark of an old land-keeping custodian, witness to the transfer in the humans' own time, and rules that a grant allowed also by an office of the island's own older law stands on ground the crossing never touched.

title: The Coombes and the Pettifers found for the holders
body: Two of the seventeen suits at Ceann mhòr, each carrying a custodian's old countersign on its title, are found whole for the families that hold them, the only two of the assize's nineteen causes decided against the Crown that summer.

title: Walter Hale heard as a witness at Ceann mhòr
body: Having no standing to plead, Walter Hale is called instead to the bench as a witness, and shows Eilidh nic Leòid the Moot's own minute of a family's land divided by agreement and set down in writing years before, which the court accepts over the memory of the parties themselves.

title: The Moot's minute-books credited by a Crown bench
body: Eilidh nic Leòid rules that a record kept by a body the Crown does not recognise is no less a fact for the hand that wrote it holding no seal, the first time the Moot's own paper is taken as evidence before a circuit justice.

title: Hale and Eilidh nic Leòid speak at the Ceann mhòr inn
body: Over supper Walter Hale asks Eilidh nic Leòid whether an exact law can also be a fair one; she tells him plainly that she made her ruling to be exact rather than kind, and that she knows whose convenience it was written to serve, a thing she has told no maor and no council chest.

title: Eilidh nic Leòid begins the gathered book
body: Through the winter after the Ceann mhòr sitting, Eilidh nic Leòid sets down in one book the whole of her nine years' rulings on Tuathaich land, from the Seann Bhral ruling to the seventeen suits, so that a justice after her need not dig the council's own chests to learn what she already knows.

title: Eilidh nic Leòid at the Seann Bhral harbour wall
body: Riding on from Àth leathan by the western road after the Ceann mhòr assize, Eilidh nic Leòid stands a while before the light fails at the harbour wall of Seann Bhral in the west, where she gave the Leòid ruling seven years before, and says nothing of it to Murchadh Clàrc.

title: Eilidh nic Leòid dies
body: Eilidh nic Leòid dies at Cathair dhomhain. Her rulings are bound in one book, the first law-book of the restored kingdom, and every circuit justice after her carries a copy.

title: Eilidh nic Leòid sends for Uilleam mac Leòid
body: Failing through am Màrt, Eilidh nic Leòid sends word north to her brother's son Uilleam, a young man who has ridden the northern circuit with her twice as a boy, asking him to take up the circuit she can no longer ride.

title: Eilidh nic Leòid dies at Cathair dhomhain
body: Eilidh nic Leòid dies in her own house within sound of the harbour, her clerk Murchadh Clàrc beside her and the gathered book of her rulings finished but not yet bound on the table by the bed.

title: Leabhar nam Breith bound
body: The council's own binder binds Eilidh nic Leòid's gathered rulings in plain calf under the name she chose for it herself, Leabhar nam Breith, and every circuit justice after her is given a copy to carry.

title: Uilleam mac Leòid named to the northern circuit
body: Uilleam mac Leòid is named circuit justice of the north in his aunt's place, and rides for his first assize with Leabhar nam Breith strapped behind his clerk's saddle, as the satchel of blank record-books was once strapped behind his aunt's.

title: Leabharlann Muileann chaol founded
body: A great library is founded at Muileann chaol. In time it holds the fullest record of the island's past that has come down.

title: Ailean Leabhar, first keeper
body: Ailean mac Iain, called Ailean Leabhar, is made the first keeper of Leabharlann Muileann chaol. He brings with him the council's minute-books and what is left of the humans' tithe ledgers, takes in the custodians' rolls kept in the town's cellars since the Severance war, and spends his first years having them read.

title: A chur san Leabharlann
body: Within a few years 'a chur san Leabharlann', to put it in the Library, is said of anything settled beyond dispute. Ailean Leabhar is said to have disliked the phrase, for the Library settles nothing, he said, and only keeps.

title: Ailean mac Iain named first keeper of the Library
body: By the council's own sentence, Ailean mac Iain is named keeper of the record at Muileann chaol, to receive, to order, and to keep whatever is sent to him. The office has no precedent and the warrant no further words, leaving Ailean to learn from the town itself what a keeper of a record might be.

title: The custodians' rolls found under Muileann chaol
body: The town's own custodians lead Ailean Leabhar down a stair to a wet cellar under the old grain-store, where rolls and bound books have stood on planks above standing water since before the Severance, the lowest tier gone soft as bread. He reads three lines by the light thrown down the stair, then sends for lamps and a table.

title: Coinneach Clàrc taken on at the Library
body: A wright's orphaned son of Muileann chaol, thirteen that spring and hired out by his mother for whatever a household could spare, attaches himself to Ailean Leabhar's carts on their first afternoon in the town and is set to fetch and carry, and within the year to read a Mission hand that few south of the guard-line can any longer make out.

title: The council's minute-books sent east to the Library
body: Four sacks of the council's own minute-books, and behind them the boxed and charred tithe ledgers of the humans' counting-houses that Ailean boxed unread fourteen years before, are carried east from Cathair dhearg to Muileann chaol, the first of the kingdom's scattered papers to be gathered into one keeping.

title: The Library's first reading room opened
body: Ailean Leabhar opens a dry chamber above the cellar to any who can show a letter from a shire maor vouching for their errand, on the plain reasoning that a Library nobody can reach is no better kept than a cellar nobody can reach. For the better part of a year it stands empty of anyone but his own copyists.

title: The first readers
body: The library's first reading room is opened to any who can show a letter from a shire maor. The first reader written in its book is a shipwright of Ros dhomhain, who asks for the humans' plans of their hulls.

title: The bath-house at the hot springs
body: A new bath-house is built over the hot springs near Muileann ruadh, paid for by the Guild of Hewers for miners sick with the dust. The guild's sick-roll for its first year names four hundred men by name and shift.

title: The keepers of the five lights
body: The five lighthouses built under the humans are given Dia-thìrich keepers by royal warrant. At Taigh-solais Baile chrom on the Tuathaich coast the keeper is a Dia-thìreach man lodged in a Tuathaich town, and his warrant bids him report what he sees on land as well as at sea.

title: The Muileann chaol town grows
body: Copyists, binders and paper-makers settle at Muileann chaol about the library. The town is granted a market charter, and its first market day is held in the library's yard.

title: The Library's copyists turn every date to the civil calendar
body: Ailean Leabhar sets his copyists to turning every date the cellar and the tithe ledgers hold into the civil calendar the humans brought, disliking the old count of the Diosal, which runs backward into the thousands and names every year after the day the humans' kin went over the water.

title: The Age of Ailean parted from the eldest age
body: Laying the tellings of Clann na Ceiste against the king-lists the custodians' rolls preserve, Ailean Leabhar's reckoners find that nearly half of the copyists' eldest age falls within the single life of Ailean Mòr, and by the consent of all seven copyists that life is counted an age of its own, the first change the Library makes to any reckoning it did not itself invent.

title: "A chur san Leabharlann" first said at Muileann chaol
body: A council clerk, told that a boundary query will want weeks of reading before it can be honestly answered, says the matter can simply be put in the Library and left settled. Ailean Leabhar corrects him sharply, and the correction, carried home and retold, is what fixes the phrase in the town's mouth rather than loosening it.

title: Cailean mac Eachainn's Line of Aisling found in the margin
body: Copying a camp roll of Àth ìseal a third time, Coinneach Clàrc notices a second, later hand in its margin: Cailean mac Eachainn's line of descent, the Line of Aisling, set down a great many years before. Ailean Leabhar has it copied fair within the week.

title: Leabhar nan Sloinnidhean opened
body: Ailean Leabhar begins a book for nothing but lines of descent, naming it Leabhar nan Sloinnidhean, the book of lines, and sets Cailean mac Eachainn's Line of Aisling in it directly after the older Line of the Mason, found wedged behind a shifted course of brick in the same cellar.

title: Leabhar nan Aithrisean opened
body: Where the Àth ìseal roll's margin also keeps tales set down by firelight rather than by day, the Hollow Man, the white stag, a captain's boast of a wolf and a door held alone, Ailean Leabhar opens a second book, Leabhar nan Aithrisean, the book of tellings, and enters the long years of Ailean Mòr and his children beside them without correction.

title: A Ros dhomhain shipwright first signs the reading-book
body: A shipwright of Ros dhomhain walks the coast road with a maor's letter to ask whether the humans ever set down the true lines of a hull. Ailean Leabhar finds three drawings folded inside an unrelated survey, and the shipwright copies them out over four days, the first name entered in the Library's reading-book.

title: The Guild of Hewers' bath-house built at the warm springs
body: The Guild of Hewers builds a bath-house of its own funds over the hot springs below Muileann ruadh, for men the pits have made sick with the dust, and sends the Library its first sick-roll unasked: four hundred men named by shift and by face of the pit that broke them.

title: The five lighthouses given Dia-thìreach keepers
body: By royal warrant the five lighthouses built under the humans are given keepers of the kingdom's own naming. Ailean Leabhar drafts all five, the four southern warrants alike and the fifth, for Baile chrom on the Tuathaich coast, bidding its keeper report what he sees by land as well as by sea.

title: The keeper's light lit at Baile chrom
body: A Dia-thìreach keeper who asked for the northern posting himself takes up the light at Baile chrom, among a Tuathaich town that has never before had a Dia-thìreach man set to live and watch among it. The southern four lights draw no comment; the fifth draws only silence that first season.

title: The market entered in the Library's register
body: Ailean Leabhar enters the market granted to Muileann chaol in the Library's own register, its stall-fee a penny a table and its first court kept by a wright's widow with a length of string, the first entry in that book to concern the town rather than the record.

title: Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill sent to inspect the Library at Muileann chaol
body: The council sends its under-clerk Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill, four-and-forty, to see and report on the record Ailean Leabhar has kept at Muileann chaol since its founding, the errand falling to her only for want of causes on her own desk that month.

title: Muileann chaol granted a market charter
body: The district's maor writes up, at the keeper's own asking, that a town which has drawn copyists, binders and paper-makers to it in two years without leave might as well be given a charter before its own trade sets its rules instead. The council grants it in the usual form, a fee for every stall and a court to hear the fair's disputes.

title: The first market day held in the Library's yard
body: Thirty stalls of thread, nails, candles and the district's own produce are set up on trestles against the Library's wall, the stall-fee a penny a table paid into a box the keeper's boy carries, and the fair's own court amounting to the boy's mother settling disputes over table-space in a voice heard the length of the yard.

title: The Tobar dhìreach mill's first delivery reaches the Library
body: Forty quires of the new paper-mill's paper are carried up the road on a borrowed cart, better and cheaper, by the copyists' own judgement, than anything the council's stationers at Cathair dhearg have sent north; within the year near enough every sheet the Library uses comes from the one stream.

title: The paper-mill at Tobar dhìreach
body: A paper-mill is built at Tobar dhìreach, a few miles from the library, on the stream below the village. For half a century nearly every page of the royal chronicle is written on its paper.

title: The first royal chronicler appointed
body: An office is made to keep the records of the kingdom. From it comes the archive whence these annals are drawn.

title: The years counted by the ages
body: With the office of chronicler the council orders that the kingdom's records shall count their years no longer by the Diosal but by the ages of the library's table, each age from its own first event: six ages as the table then stands, and seven since the Dubhan Era. The chronicler's first year is entered as the eighteenth of the Severance Era. Thereafter the count of the Diosal is kept only in old books.

title: Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill
body: The first royal chronicler is Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill, a clerk of the council. She keeps her record at Muileann chaol and not at the capital, and writes in her first entry that a record kept beside the throne is kept for the throne.

title: The office of royal chronicler set at Muileann chaol, not the capital
body: Sworn into the new office at Cathair dhearg and given no instruction as to its seat, Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill writes back within the week that she means to keep the record at Muileann chaol, beside the Library that already holds the rolls and the copyists the work wants, and that a record kept beside the throne is kept for the throne.

title: Gormshuil sworn royal chronicler
body: Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill is sworn royal chronicler in a small room at Cathair dhearg on the twentieth of an t-Samhain, four-and-forty, before a clerk who reads the warrant's clause on the counting of the years in the same flat voice as its clause on her seat.

title: Uilleam mac Griogair names the under-clerk
body: When the office of chronicler is made, it is Uilleam mac Griogair, clerk of council, who remembers that the under-clerk he sent to Muileann chaol came back with more to say than he had troubled to hear, and names her to it.

title: The first chronicle circuit
body: Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill sends clerks to every shire to copy parish books, grave-lists and harbour rolls. The returns from the south fill forty chests. The returns from Siorrachd Àth àrsaidh and the other northern shires fill one, for few Tuathaich will speak to the clerks.

title: The town arms copied
body: The clerks of the first chronicle circuit copy the seal of every town they visit into the roll of arms, and the roll comes to hold the arms of five hundred and five places. In the north most are copied from the humans' old town seals, for few Tuathaich will show the clerks their own.

title: The chest from Inis bheag
body: At Inis bheag in the north-east the chronicle clerks are shown a parish book that goes back before the coming of the humans, kept in the Seann Spioradan house there. The keeper lets it be copied, and not taken.

title: Boats lost off Cuan bheag
body: A storm out of the west drowns eleven Tuathaich fishermen off Cuan bheag in the north. The village has no lifeboat. The Moot buys one by subscription and asks the council to pay half; the council pays a third.

title: Tormod mac Sheumais joins the first chronicle circuit
body: A council under-clerk's son of three-and-thirty, called already Tormod Pinn for the speed of his hand, asks Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill for a place on the first circuit rather than wait to be sent, and rides the northern half of it.

title: The town arms of five hundred and five burghs copied into one book
body: The chronicle circuit's southern chests yield the town arms of every burgh that has ever cut a seal, five hundred and five of them, entered by Coinneach Clàrc in the order the chests happen to arrive rather than by rank, on Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill's own ruling that a tidied record forgets how untidy its own arrival was.

title: The chronicle clerks turned away at Doire ghlas
body: Tormod mac Sheumais reads the circuit's own warrant twice aloud in the street at the harbour agent's demand before he is let copy a single ledger; eleven of the town's twelve doors stay closed against him, an answer he judges memory rather than unkindness.

title: The Inis bheag keeper lets his parish book be copied and not carried
body: The old keeper of the Seann Spioradan house at Inis bheag hears the circuit's warrant once, without asking it twice, and lets his parish roll be copied at his own table under his own eye, but will not let the book itself travel so much as to the harbour, telling the clerk that a book kept that many generations belongs to the house and not to any seal.

title: The northern chest opened: the maor's returns and nothing more
body: Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill opens the one chest the northern shires have filled and finds only the maor of Siorrachd Àth àrsaidh's own tallies and licences, not a line in it written by a Tuathaich hand; she enters the fact plainly and adds no further word to it.

title: The chronicle clerks ride out in three pairs
body: In the spring the first chronicle circuit's clerks ride out in three pairs, one south, one to the eastern shires nearer the mountain and one north past Cnoc ghorm to the Tuathaich coast, each pair with its own warrant and its own chest to fill.

title: Thomas Coyle drowned off Cuan bheag
body: A westerly storm on the second night of an t-Sultain drowns eleven Tuathaich fishermen out of Cuan bheag, Thomas Coyle of Caol mhòr among them, one-and-forty and near twenty years married to Mary Coyle. The sea gives back two broken hulls and a stranger's oar; the town buries what it can within the week.

title: Mary Coyle's roll of the eleven dead
body: Mary Coyle, newly widowed, writes the eleven drowned men's names out on a single sheet for the mason's stones, setting them in the order the boats went out rather than the order the sea gave the bodies back, holding that order the truer one.

title: The Moot opens its lifeboat subscription
body: Walter Hale carries the wreck's news to the Moot's own council at Caol mhòr, which votes that same evening to open a subscription for a lifeboat at Cuan bheag; Hale opens the list himself, and it carries near two hundred names by the month's end. The council, asked to bear half the cost, answers four months on that it will bear a third.

title: The tale of the Sea-Watcher told to the chronicler
body: A fisherman out of Achadh àrsaidh, at the summer bothies below the cold cape, tells the royal chronicler Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill the coast's own tale of a shape seen off the cold cape, seen always at a distance and never named by those who fear it, which she enters in the book that keeps what people said rather than the book that keeps names.

title: The raiders' anchorage noted at the cold cape
body: The same fisherman tells Gormshuil that the flagless ships working those waters know the cold cape's currents better than any stranger crew should, and keep some hidden anchorage among its rocks; she writes it apart from the tale and asks that the council's coastal watch be told of it.

title: The flocks of Eilean dhubh counted by their own hands
body: A treasury clerk sent to number the flocks of Eilean dhubh for the head-due finds the islanders unwilling to have him count their own pastures, and takes instead their sworn count by tally-stick, on which the island's dues are set that year and every year after.

title: The eleven stones set at Cuan bheag
body: The mason of Cuan bheag cuts and sets eleven stones for the drowned from Mary Coyle's single sheet, in the order the boats went out, and they stand weathering by the jetty when the lifeboat is put into the water the spring after.

title: The thing off the north-west cape
body: Fishermen out of Achadh àrsaidh tell of a creature longer than their boats in the waters off the north-west cape. Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill writes down the tale, and adds that the raiders shelter in those same waters.

title: The Eilean dhubh sheep-count
body: A royal clerk is sent to count the flocks of Eilean dhubh, greatest of the outer isles, to set the island's dues. The islanders count them for him, and the dues are set on their count.

title: Cathair gheal arms its boats
body: The Tuathaich fishermen of Cathair gheal arm their own boats and drive the raiders from the bay. Twice they had asked the council for help, and none was sent. Afterwards the council fines the town for bearing arms without licence, and the fine is paid.

title: The market cross at Cathair mhòr
body: A market cross is raised at Cathair mhòr at the cost of the house of Mac Ùisdein, with the house's name cut on all four faces. The town's wool and coal markets are moved to its foot.

title: The Cuan bheag lifeboat launched
body: The lifeboat ordered of the Cuan shean yard comes up the coast in an Cèitean and is set afloat off Cuan bheag's jetty by the hands of that autumn's five widows, no priest of either faith having an agreed form to bless a boat neither had built.

title: Nell Barrow's first letter for Cathair gheal
body: Nell Barrow, a skipper's widow of Cathair gheal who has lost a nephew to the raiders, writes the town's case to the council in am Faoilleach, asking a boat armed at the council's expense or leave to arm the town's own; the maor warns her plain words are as likely filed as answered. No answer comes.

title: Nell Barrow's second letter for Cathair gheal
body: Two months unanswered, Nell Barrow writes a second letter in am Màrt, shorter and plainer than the first, ending that the town does not think a third asking will find the council less occupied than the first two were. It too goes unanswered.

title: The black ship run aground in Cathair gheal's bay
body: On the night of 8 an Giblean three flagless hulls stand into Cathair gheal's bay; the largest raider ship runs her keel onto a shifted bar and is boarded and burned by seven town boats before dawn, the two lesser hulls standing off rather than come to her aid.

title: Two dead and four hurt in the bay's clearing
body: The fight for Cathair gheal's bay costs the town two men dead and four hurt, one of whom keeps no further use of a hand; Nell Barrow herself takes a burn from a fallen lantern that scars her the rest of her life, and by first light tells the town the bay is clear.

title: Cathair gheal fined for bearing arms unlicensed
body: The council's ruling on the night's fight names no boat sent and no licence granted, only that Cathair gheal bore arms without leave first asked, and fines the town four purses of the realm-coin, to be paid at the maor's own office before the year's dues fall due.

title: Walter Hale carries the Moot's purse north to Cathair gheal
body: Hearing the town lacks two-thirds of its fine, Walter Hale carries the difference north from the Moot's own purse, the same purse the Cuan bheag lifeboat has already thinned, and reaches Cathair gheal near the end of an t-Iuchar.

title: The fine paid at the maor's door
body: Nell Barrow's sum and Hale's together clear the fine in full at the maor's own door, counted coin by coin before his clerk, who enters the sum received and asks nothing of the six years, the two letters, or the boat the town was never sent.

title: Ellen Hale dies at Caol mhòr
body: Ellen Hale, Walter Hale's wife, dies at Caol mhòr in the second week of an Lùnastal at seventy, in the loft the family had lodged in since the boat brought them north; the Moot's day-book gives the day and the hour, and beneath them David's line that the Moot did not sit that week.

title: Ellen Hale buried on the rise above the harbour
body: Ellen Hale is buried on the rise above Caol mhòr's harbour with the fishwives, the Carrick women, the widows of the Cuan bheag drowning and the whole of the Moot's council standing by; the minister reads the twenty-third psalm, from which she had taught her children their letters, and her husband says nothing aloud.

title: Crosses and lifeboats
body: Hearing the council's long minute on the Mac Ùisdein market cross read at the Moot's table beside its short one on Cathair gheal's fine, Mary Coyle says that the council seems to know a great deal about crosses and rather less about lifeboats, and goes back to counting the boats home.

title: The house of the Stone at Caol leathan
body: The house of Òrd na Cloiche at Caol leathan, greatest of the order, is rebuilt with a tower, and a bell rings the hours from it. The town sets its market and its courts by the bell.

title: Fèill Muileann òg first held
body: A fair is held each year at Muileann òg, and it becomes the greatest gathering on the island. Trade comes to it from every province the state holds.

title: Oighrig nic Mhathain's rules
body: Oighrig nic Mhathain, first toll-mistress of the fair at Muileann òg, sets its rules: a stall-fee in coin, a court of the fair for disputes, and Tuathaich goods to be sold only through Dia-thìrich factors. The rules are read aloud at the opening of every fair to this day.

title: The fair's road
body: The road from Cathair dhearg to Muileann òg is widened and metalled for the carts of the fair. It passes Dùn chrom, which takes a toll at its gate and grows on it. As far as Muileann ghlas it runs on the old coal road; the new stretches are called Rathad na Fèille.

title: The Stone's house at Caol leathan rebuilt
body: The order of the Stone rebuilds its house at Caol leathan at its own cost, raising a bell tower over the western gable; the town sets its market and its two courts by the bell from that year on.

title: Oighrig nic Mhathain named toll-mistress
body: Oighrig nic Mhathain, nine years the market clerk of Dùn chrom and one-and-thirty that year, is asked by the council's eastern factor to keep the new fair to be held at the ford by Muileann òg, and takes the post, leaving her own scales to a niece she has trained two summers at her elbow.

title: The fair-field marked out at Muileann òg
body: Oighrig nic Mhathain walks the ground at Muileann òg with a length of cord and a stick through the summer, marking the stalls, the beast-pens and the corner where a court might sit, before any building has been raised there.

title: The court of the fair roofed
body: Carpenters of Dùn chrom finish a plain roofed frame, open on three sides, at the field's corner nearest the ford, a fortnight before the fair is to open; it is the only building the state gives the fair in its first year.

title: Oighrig writes the fair's three rules
body: Over three evenings by rush-light Oighrig nic Mhathain writes the fair's rules in her own plain hand: a stall-fee in coin, a court of the fair to sit each day of the gathering, and Tuathaich goods to be sold only through licensed Dia-thìreach factors, on the council's own instruction.

title: The first factors licensed for northern goods
body: The council licenses four merchant houses of the eastern shires to stand factors' stalls at Muileann òg and sell Tuathaich goods under their own names for a share of the price; Oighrig nic Mhathain enters their names under a heading of her own, Bàillidhean na Fèille.

title: The court of the fair's first sitting
body: On the fair's opening morning, 16 an Dàmhair, Oighrig nic Mhathain's court hears its first case, a dispute over a barrel of salt fish, and settles it within the hour by weighing the barrel herself; she writes it into her book as setting the pattern for every case after it.

title: The spoil-stone case judged by a smith's eye
body: A Cathair mhòr coal-carter brings a Sloc Mòr merchant's load of spoil-stone dressed to pass for coal-iron before the court of the fair; Oighrig nic Mhathain, having no forge of her own, sends the load to Muileann òg's one smith and fines the merchant by his judgment.

title: David Hale's wool turned away at the gate
body: David Hale of Caol mhòr brings four sacks of his father's wool to the fair's ninth day, the first cart from the Moot's own provinces to try it; Oighrig nic Mhathain reads him her own third clause and turns him to a factor's stall, where his wool sells for some fifth part less than a northern market would have given.

title: The first fair runs a fortnight
body: The first fair at Muileann òg runs a fortnight, with wool from the western shires, the Sloc Mòr's coal from the east, Baile chiar's cloth and salt from the coastal pans on the one field, more trade than Oighrig nic Mhathain had seen gathered in nine years of market days.

title: Pipers from Baile chiar at the first fair
body: Pipers from Baile chiar play for coin at the far corner of the first fair's field, over the woodsmoke and wet wool and the coal carts' black dust, through the low constant argument of buying and selling in half a dozen tongues.

title: Dùn chrom's gate-toll
body: The toll taken at Dùn chrom's gate on the fair road pays for a new wall on the town's southern side. The townsfolk call it the fair's wall. The carters of the fair call it something else.

title: Niall dies; Brìghde crowned
body: Niall dies, and his daughter Brìghde follows him without contest: a mortal heir passing to a mortal heir among a nobility some of whom never age. It was thought no wonder then. It was thought one later.

title: The chronicler's use of the saying
body: Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill writes that the succession came 'mar a thàinig Niall'; it is the first time the saying is found in the royal record. In all her years as chronicler she lets no other idiom into the chronicle.

title: The ancestors' hall at Seann Dunn
body: The Seann Spioradan houses of the east coast build a common hall at Seann Dunn, where each year the living heads of forty families name their ancestors aloud. The next year the list is copied to the library, and it grows by a few names every year after.

title: The fair's road metalled past Dùn chrom
body: In am Faoilleach the last stretch of the road from Cathair dhearg to Muileann òg is metalled for the fair's carts; the carters already call it Rathad na Fèille before the state gives it a name of its own.

title: Dùn chrom's gate-toll raises the fair's wall
body: The toll taken at Dùn chrom's gate on the fair's road pays, that same winter, for a new wall along the town's southern side, finished by an Cèitean; the townsfolk call it the fair's wall, and the carters call the gate by another name.

title: The Moot's letter against the factor rule filed
body: Walter Hale writes to the council on the Moot's behalf naming the factor rule a licence laid across a trade the north carried on unaided, and asks it looked at again; the council answers, months on, that the rule stands and will not be reconsidered inside the year, and the letter is filed with the Moot's earlier ones.

title: The fair's rules confirmed and read aloud
body: In an Lùnastal a council clerk reads Oighrig nic Mhathain's rules aloud before the gathered factors and maoir of the eastern shires, word for word as she wrote them, and asks whether the reading matches her own book; she tells him it does.

title: The bells rung for Niall
body: The bells of Òrd Mhacha at Cathair dhearg are rung a full day and a night for Niall's death, and the capital keeps no market. The crowd that gathers is the largest since his crowning; it stays quiet, and disperses before the second night.

title: The council's oath sworn afresh
body: The council of twelve, sitting on its fixed day within the week of the crowning, swears its oath of service afresh before Brìghde. The minute-book gives it one line among the day's ordinary business and no more.

title: The corrected proclamation at Ros dhomhain
body: A harbour clerk at Ros dhomhain, copying the crowning's proclamation for the gate, writes Niall's name from habit, scores it through, and sets Brìghde's above the line. The corrected copy is kept under glass at the gate.

title: Gormshuil's struck drafts
body: The chronicler writes and rejects three entries for the crowning before any stands: one too bare, one that says more than an office should say first, one left unfinished as an argument rather than a record. All three are struck through in her working book.

title: Gormshuil's resolve on the one idiom
body: Having let *mar a thàinig Niall* into the royal record, the chronicler resolves to admit no other such phrase for as long as the office is hers, having seen other offices lose their plainness one borrowed ornament at a time.

title: The hall raised at Seann Dunn
body: Forty households of the Seann Spioradan along the east coast raise a common hall at Seann Dunn in a single season, working the stone by day, and roof it before the first frost. It holds no image or carving, only two hearths.

title: Gormshuil's visit to the first naming
body: The chronicler rides east to Seann Dunn to watch the hall's first naming of ancestors, not on the Library's business but her own, her mother's house keeping the same rite at a hearth too small for half its dead.

title: The Library's offer to Seann Dunn
body: Asked by an elder of the hall whether the Library keeps such lists of the dead, Gormshuil answers that it does not, but will keep any copy sent to it as carefully as anything else that reaches Muileann chaol.

title: The vote for a light at Cuan ruadh
body: After two boats are lost on the harbour rocks in a winter fog, the town council of Cuan ruadh votes its own coal money to burn a light on the mole where no Board light has ever reached.

title: Gormshuil's mother laughs at the idiom
body: Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill's mother, hearing in her village by Ceann àrsaidh that her daughter has let mar a thàinig Niall into the royal record, laughs longer than Gormshuil thinks the thing deserves, and says her daughter spent years learning to write like nobody in particular so that she could in the end write like everybody.

title: Nine generations named at Seann Dunn
body: At the first naming in the hall at Seann Dunn an old woman of the town recites nine generations of her dead before her voice gives out, and her son speaks the tenth for her.

title: Cuan ruadh's harbour light
body: Cuan ruadh on the east coast, which has none of the five lighthouses, raises a harbour light of its own on the mole and burns in it coal bought by the town. The Lighthouse Board will not take it on.

title: Còmhrag Ceann leathan first fought
body: A fierce melee is first fought at Ceann leathan, and is fought there every year after. It is held to be a martial custom. More and more it is where a people with few other outlets spend their anger.

title: Calum Ruadh
body: The first champion of the Còmhrag whose name is remembered is Calum mac Aonghais, called Calum Ruadh, a hewer of Muileann chrom. Two men die in the melee he wins. The prize is a year's wages and the right to bear arms in any shire.

title: Ceann leathan's inns
body: Ceann leathan builds four new inns for the crowds of the Còmhrag. The fair-wardens of the town, who take a share of every room, become the Còmhrag's keepers in all but name.

title: The Seann Dunn list first copied to the Library
body: The hall at Seann Dunn sends the Library the first copy of its naming, and goes on sending one every year after, each a little longer than the last. Gormshuil enters only the day it came and the count of names.

title: The Lighthouse Board's refusal
body: The Comhairle nan Taighean-solais writes back to Cuan ruadh that its charter names five lights and no more, and that the town's own light, being no charge on the Crown, may continue as it is. Gormshuil enters the refusal in four lines.

title: The rules of the first Còmhrag
body: The first Còmhrag at Ceann leathan is fought under rules that run to little more than a fee, a bar on edged weapons, and a purse for the last man standing inside the ropes. Nobody thinks the custom will need more than that.

title: The dead of the first Còmhrag buried
body: Two men who do not walk out of the ropes at the first Còmhrag are buried at Ceann leathan within the week. The melee is fought again the following summer regardless, and the record gives their deaths one plain sentence.

title: Calum Ruadh's purse counted out
body: A year's wages are counted out on a trestle table by the fair-wardens' own clerk for Calum mac Aonghais, hewer of Muileann chrom, who wins the first Còmhrag by refusing to stay down.

title: The right to bear arms entered on the shire's roll
body: Calum Ruadh's right to bear arms in any shire of the kingdom, the Còmhrag's second prize, is entered that same evening on the shire's roll at Ceann leathan, a right his own father never held.

title: The fair-wardens' free table
body: The inn-keepers of Ceann leathan, four of whom built new houses that year for the Còmhrag's crowds, keep Calum Ruadh's table free of charge, a custom nobody formally agrees to but that holds for as long as he comes back to fight.

title: Calum Ruadh walks home alone
body: Calum Ruadh walks out of Ceann leathan before dawn the morning after the first Còmhrag with the purse in his coat and the shire clerk's paper folded inside it, past the shuttered inns and the field where the ropes were taken down in the night, and takes the coal road north toward Muileann chrom alone.

title: The grain-ships of Ros gheal
body: Ros gheal on the north-central coast builds a dock for the grain-ships of the Hawk country. The Hawk houses bless the dock and ask a tithe of its dues. The shire gives them a twentieth.

title: Mary Coyle first speaks in the Moot
body: Mary Coyle, widowed of the Cuan bheag drowning, stands and speaks her own words in the Moot at Caol mhòr rather than sending a note forward to be read by another. The clerk David Hale sets her speech down whole in the day-book, the first time a woman's words are kept there entire rather than summed in a line.

title: Splatter and Dodge's generation born
body: Many children are born in these years to the shunting families of the yard. From them come Seachran and Brean and others of that generation, who grow up to be Dubhan's closest allies.

title: Seann Bhral in the south
body: Seann Bhral on the south coast, not the town of that name in the west, becomes the greatest fishing port of the kingdom and lands more fish than Ros dhomhain. Its curing-sheds run the length of the harbour.

title: The widows heard first
body: The Moot resolves that the widows of the drowned be heard on the same footing as any man who has paid his shilling, and heard first when a matter touches their own dead. The rule is entered as standing, not as a courtesy for one night, on the widow Agnes Tulloch's motion.

title: The Hawk's twentieth first paid
body: Ros gheal's factor pays the Hawk houses their first quarter's twentieth on the dues of the new grain dock, the sum the shire's factor haggled down from a tithe. The due is paid every quarter after, and the clerks of Ros gheal come to call it simply the Hawk's, few remembering why.

title: The circus at Seann Chwen
body: The travelling show that calls itself An Siorcas Siubhail Do-thuigsinn is first recorded, pitched near Seann Chwen on the southern coast. The chronicler's clerk could not say what its acts were meant to show. Nor, he adds, could the crowd, and it came back the next night.

title: Manannan's feast at Seann Bhral
body: The house of Òrd Mhanannain at Seann Bhral, one of the oldest on the west coast, will not admit the Tuathaich from the north who come to its feast of the sea, as their forebears learned to do from the Dia-thìrich harbours. Its keeper says the sea is the same and the house is not.

title: The Moot votes to send the western crossing
body: After two hard sittings the Moot agrees to Mary Coyle's asking, that northern boats sail west-about to keep the sea-feast at Seann Bhral where the Tuathaich forebears once kept it. Many in the room call it a fool's errand for winter, and are not silenced, only outvoted.

title: Eleven boats sail for Seann Bhral
body: Eleven boats out of Caol mhòr, Cuan bheag and Ros mhòr put out on a grey morning at the end of an Lùnastal under Mary Coyle, carrying little but themselves, a keg of salt fish apiece, and the Moot's own sheet naming her their word. Ros bheag's harbour will not give them its quay, and sends them to a mooring buoy instead.

title: A boat nearly lost off the passage
body: A squall out of the south-west puts green water over the bow of the smallest boat of the eleven, and its crew bails her clear with whatever will hold water. No one of the fleet is lost on the four days' passage, though more than one aboard call it the hardest going since the Crossing itself.

title: The house at Seann Bhral answers Mary Coyle
body: The keeper of Manannan's order at Seann Bhral in the west hears Mary Coyle's asking through to the end and refuses it: the house is kept on tithes of families who hold the rite by blood and the custodian's book, and cannot be opened on a four days' claim, however justly sailed. He tells her the sea is the same; the house is not.

title: Mary Coyle resolves to keep the feast at Cnoc ghorm
body: On the passage home Mary Coyle tells the crews the north will keep the feast of the sea itself, in full, at the church above Cnoc ghorm where a thin blessing of the boats is already kept each spring. The decision is made before the eleven boats raise Caol mhòr again.

title: A Ros mhòr man asks what now
body: On the third day home from Seann Bhral, off the northern capes, an old Ros mhòr hand who has said little the whole voyage asks Mary Coyle plainly what she means to do now that the west will not have them.

title: The northern sea-feast
body: Turned away at Seann Bhral, the Tuathaich keep the feast at the church at Cnoc ghorm instead, as a blessing of the boats. They keep it there every year after, and within a generation the northern feast is greater than the western.

title: The first Fleadh na Mara kept in full
body: More than fifty boats gather at Cnoc ghorm on the second Sunday of an Gearran, far beyond any year before, and the parish priest blesses each hull in turn with heather dipped in harbour water. Mary Coyle's own boat, which carried her to Seann Bhral and back, is blessed fourth in the row.

title: David Hale counts the boats at Cnoc ghorm
body: David Hale keeps a written count of the boats blessed at Cnoc ghorm for the Moot's day-book, the first such count taken of the feast. Word of the gathering's size travels the north coast faster than the crossing to Seann Bhral had, and boats are promised from as far as Inis mhin's country the year after.

title: The Depletion first noted
body: The survey reports begin to note, without remark, that the vein yields less. For years the state does nothing.

title: Iain Mapa's survey
body: The survey behind the report is the work of Iain mac Ruairidh, called Iain Mapa, of the Mine Board. His measures of the faces of the Sloc Mòr show the vein thinning to east and south. The Board files the survey and shows it to no one, and Iain Mapa is sent to the silver works at Muileann chiar.

title: Iain Mapa true up the eastern faces
body: Sent into the eastern galleries of the Sloc Mòr to settle a dispute between two overseers over a cutting's bounds, the chainman Iain mac Ruairidh, called Iain Mapa, checks an old survey against the new digging and finds the figures will not lie flat. He walks the faces a second time before he trusts what they tell him.

title: The vein found thinning east and south
body: A third survey of the faces gives Iain Mapa the same figures as the first two, to within an inch the chain itself can account for: the vein runs narrower to the east than the old maps show, and pinches again to the south. He sets it down in a hand that does not shake, and does not argue.

title: Iain Mapa walks the survey to Cathair dhearg
body: Rather than trust the carters with a finding he believes the Board should see in his own hand, Iain Mapa rolls and ties his survey and walks the thirty-one miles from the Sloc Mòr to Cathair dhearg in a day and a half, sleeping one night on the road, and tells no one at the mine beforehand what the sheet holds.

title: The Board leaves the survey unrolled
body: Iain Mapa lays his survey before three men of the Mine Board at Cathair dhearg and unties the string himself. None of the three unrolls it. He gives them the finding by mouth, plainly, and is told only, by the one in the middle, that it will be considered.

title: Ruairidh mac Ailein signs the receipt
body: Asked for a receipt for the survey he has carried in, Iain Mapa is given four written lines naming nothing of the finding, only that a survey was received and filed. Ruairidh mac Ailein of the Board signs it, since the man in the middle will not, and Iain Mapa folds it into his pocket-book.

title: The survey filed and shown to no one
body: Within the week Iain Mapa's survey is filed in the Board's own press at Cathair dhearg with the two years' surveys before it, and circulated to no one on the council or in any other office of the state. It lies there unread while the men who might have acted on it go on believing the mountain gives as freely as ever.

title: Iain Mapa posted to Muileann chiar
body: Within the month Iain Mapa is told, with little explanation offered and none asked for, that he is wanted at the silver works at Muileann chiar, twenty-four miles east and a little south of the Sloc Mòr, where the Board has need of a man who holds a chain straight and asks no more than the work requires.

title: The boat of the field warped into the new harbour
body: Of the hulls the Great Wave cast into the fields behind Cuan dhearg two generations before, one is found sound enough to be dragged to the water, caulked and floated, and is warped into the rebuilt harbour ahead of every boat built new for it. The harbour-master keeps it moored at the quay-head as a relic rather than putting it back to work.

title: The Mine Board at Cathair mhòr
body: The Mine Board, which has sat at Cathair dhearg since the Sloc Mòr concession, moves its clerks to Cathair mhòr to be nearer the mountain. By the Board's own rule its surveys are kept there and not sent to the library.

title: The scent-makers of Seann Vell
body: The glass-houses of the capital shore begin to make small flasks, and in them the women of Seann Vell sell the waters they distil from bog-myrtle, meadowsweet and heather honey. Within a few years scent is sold in every market town, and the towns of the western plain take up the trade.

title: The Grey Night forbidden
body: A Dia-thìreach magistrate at Baile chrom forbids the gatherings of the Grey Night sect as disorderly. Hannah Crane is fined. The vigil goes indoors and goes on.

title: The harbour at Cuan dhearg reopened
body: The harbour at Cuan dhearg, lost to the Great Wave, is opened again with a new mole of dressed stone. The first boat in is one of those found in the fields behind the old town, refloated, and kept by the harbour-master as a relic.

title: The Board's clerks move to Cathair mhòr
body: The Mine Board moves its clerks and its presses the sixteen miles from Cathair dhearg to Cathair mhòr, into leased rooms above the town's wool market, on the stated ground that a board charged with the mountain's business ought to sit nearer the mountain than it had.

title: Riaghailt a' Bhùird set down
body: In four lines the Mine Board sets down, for the first time in writing, the rule that its surveyors' work is to be kept at Cathair mhòr in the Board's own presses and not sent to the Library at Muileann chaol as every other office's reports are sent. No one on the council is asked to confirm it.

title: The Moot pays Hannah Crane's fine
body: Word reaches the Moot at Caol mhòr that the vigil-keeper Hannah Crane has been fined at Baile chrom for keeping the Grey Night in the open. The Moot votes the balance of her fine out of its own small chest without much debate, on a councillor's motion that a woman fined for standing on a beach is no threat worth agreeing with.

title: The Grey Night kept indoors
body: Forbidden the open shingle below the light, the vigil of the Grey Night is kept that year in a byre lent by a family who hold the old rite themselves, one night a year, in a silence the magistrate's order cannot reach any better than it reached the shore. Outsiders are still not told which night it falls on.

title: Achadh mhin's old bounds restored
body: The shire measures the returning households of Achadh mhin back onto the same strips the humans' surveyors once cut, the old plat being the one the families still walk by memory rather than a new line drawn by a Dia-thìreach chain.

title: Achadh mhin resettled
body: The fields of Achadh mhin bear again, and a few of the families moved away after the Great Wave come back to them. The shire gives them their old bounds from the humans' survey.

title: Idle looms at Baile chiar
body: The weavers' guild of Baile chiar reports the washing-pools behind its fulling-sheds too low after a dry summer to scour wool, and its looms idle three weeks; the guild counts the bolts not woven to the last half-ell and does not count the weavers it has not paid.

title: A wedding at the Stone's door in Doire shean
body: The harbour-master of Doire shean writes to the Library of his daughter's wedding to a clerk of the Stone's counting-room, kept at the Stone's door, the first in his memory for which the whole fishing fleet came in on one tide to stand on the quay.

title: Eòghan crowned
body: Brìghde dies young, and no cause is made known. Her cousin Eòghan takes the throne, and for the first time the restored kingdom's succession is in dispute.

title: The succession entry
body: The royal chronicler's entry for the succession gives the bare fact. The chroniclers after Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill have added nothing to it.

title: Dissent recorded in council
body: For the first time the council's minutes record votes against a succession. They name the councillors who voted, and not their reasons. Two of them do not sit again.

title: The first households return to Achadh mhin
body: Three households moved off the salted fields after the Great Wave, or their children in their place, ask and are granted their old ground back, the barley coming up along strips long thought lost to the tide.

title: The twice-sealed packet reaches Muileann chaol
body: Word of Brìghde's death and Eòghan's crowning reaches the chronicler's desk in a packet sealed twice, the second hand adding, in a hastier line at the foot, that the council's own sitting on the succession did not pass as quietly as the crowning itself.

title: Gormshuil's three struck drafts
body: The chronicler writes and rejects three entries for the succession before a fourth stands: one that says more than an office should say first, one so bare it reads as a door shut on purpose, one left unfinished as an argument rather than a record.

title: The bare entry set down
body: Past the second hour of the morning Gormshuil enters the day of Brìghde's death, the fact that no cause is made known, and the day of Eòghan's crowning, and nothing more, choosing the silence rather than dressing it as a fullness it is not.

title: The council's four lines on the division
body: The council's own minute of the sitting names Tormod mac Iain Òig and Sìleas nic Artair as the two who stood against seating Eòghan, gives no reason either offered, and closes with the plainest of its four lines: the two do not sit again.

title: Tormod mac Iain Òig goes home
body: Tormod mac Iain Òig returns to his own lands in the western shires and is not named in the chronicle again for some years, his seat on the council closed behind him without further entry.

title: Sìleas nic Artair keeps her own house's rite
body: Sìleas nic Artair, her council seat lost with Tormod mac Iain Òig's, gives her Old Spirits kin's house more of her time than council business ever left her, and does not sit at Cathair dhearg again.

title: The council's two seats filled
body: Before the year turns the council seats a landed man's son from the western shires and a widow of a coastal house in the two empty places, and neither newcomer is asked in council to account for the vote that opened the seat they now hold.

title: Leabhar nam Breith cited by its page
body: Riding his twelfth year on the northern circuit, Uilleam mac Leòid finds for a Tuathaich family's grazing claim at Àth àrsaidh in the words of his aunt's ruling and cites Leabhar nam Breith by its page, the first circuit return to cite the book in its own words.

title: The Board's yield sent as a single figure
body: The Mine Board's return to the royal chronicle gives the Sloc Mòr's yield for the year as a single figure, no faces named and no survey cited; Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill enters it and sets the year before's figure beside it in her smallest hand, with no word between them.

title: The fifth copy of the Seann Dunn naming
body: The hall at Seann Dunn sends the Library its fifth copy of the naming, longer by eleven names, the hall having taken in three households of the coast that had kept their dead at their own hearths until then.

title: The warehouse quarter of Inis bhàn burns two days
body: Fire takes three storehouses and the dwellings above them at Inis bhàn on the Abhainn ìseal and burns two days before the town beats it back street by street with buckets and wet sacking; every soul in the burning quarter gets clear, and none dies.

title: Inis bhàn's fire
body: Fire takes the warehouse quarter of Inis bhàn on the Abhainn ìseal in the north-central country and burns for two days. The town's Hawk house takes in the homeless. The fire-bell the town buys afterwards is the loudest in the kingdom.

title: Dubhan born
body: Dubhan is born mortal, in the north where the Severance confined his people, decades after the war that shut the island against those from whom his line descends.

title: The Tuathaich schools counted
body: The Moot counts eleven schools in the north that teach in the humans' tongue, and three that have begun to teach Dia-thìris as well, at the parents' asking. Agnes Pike's school at Doire ghlas is one of the three.

title: The Hawk house at Inis bhàn opens its doors
body: The Hawk house at Inis bhàn, which has never before taken in households outside those sworn to it, shelters every family the fire puts out of a roof, sworn or not, through the worst of the spring cold.

title: Inis bhàn's new bell rung on the quay
body: Inis bhàn buys a bell from the founders' yard at Cathair dhearg, cast to the town's own order, to stand where the old warehouse bell burned, rung once on the quay before it is hung, and heard, by the town's own telling, further up and down the Abhainn ìseal than any bell in the kingdom.

title: The Moot's letter of the eleven schools
body: Walter Hale writes the Moot's count of the north's schools to Muileann chaol, eleven in all from Agnes Pike's byre at Doire ghlas to a room over a chandler's shop at Ceann àrsaidh opened that same autumn, and Gormshuil enters it whole rather than shortened.

title: Three schools begin teaching Dia-thìris
body: At three of the north's eleven schools the teachers begin, at the parents' own asking and with no order from the council or leave from any maor, to teach Dia-thìris alongside the humans' letters, so that children may read a proclamation or a boundary-line in the tongue the kingdom writes its business in.

title: Agnes Pike's school teaches its first Dia-thìris lesson
body: Agnes Pike's school at Doire ghlas, one of the three the Moot's letter names, sets its first Dia-thìris lesson beside the Bible and the Moot's own minutes, at the asking of the parents whose children it has taught since its founding.

title: The stone house of Mac Ùisdein
body: Uisdean mac Ùisdein's house at Cathair mhòr is rebuilt in stone quarried from the spoil of the Sloc Mòr, the greatest private house in the kingdom. The Guild of Hewers holds its feast in the new hall.

title: The Guild of Hewers feasts in the new hall
body: The Guild of Hewers holds its feast in the finished stone hall of Uisdean mac Ùisdein at Cathair mhòr, at tables set the length of the room under torches an ironsmith made to no pattern but his own, and Mòrag nic Coinnich attends as the Library's own witness.

title: The northern fishing grounds
body: Licences to fish the waters south and east of Caol mhòr are kept for Dia-thìrich boats. The Tuathaich boats are left the northern grounds, where the raiders also fish.

title: Doire shean's harbour
body: Doire shean in the south-west builds a stone harbour for the fishing boats of the Stone's country, the first new harbour since the Severance not paid for by the Crown. The house of the Stone lends the money and takes the harbour dues.

title: The mason's letter of the hall he did not sit in
body: A mason who dressed the stone of Mac Ùisdein's new hall writes the Library that he was not asked to the guild's own feast in it, his craft holding no sworn place for a cutter of stone, and Ailean Leabhar enters the letter whole rather than in his own shorter hand.

title: The first licence refused to a Caol mhòr boat
body: Sam Ridley, a Tuathaich master who has fished the southern banks off Caol mhòr eleven years, brings his catch to the maor's scales the day the new licences take force and is told the grounds are not, at present, being papered for boats of his fleet; the Moot enters the day and his name.

title: The house of the Stone takes its first quarter's dues
body: The house of the Stone at Doire shean takes its first quarter's harbour dues off the new quay before the mole's last course is dry, the sum entered beside what the house first lent the town for the building of it.

title: Trenches at Làrach an Dùin
body: Diggers sent by the library open trenches at Làrach an Dùin on the south-east coast. They find walls older than any Dia-thìreach building, and no writing at all. Ailean Leabhar has the finds entered as of the Old Ones, purpose unknown.

title: Beathag asks that the temple's ground be left
body: Beathag, eldest of three Seann Spioradan elders of the district, meets Ailean Leabhar at Làrach an Teampaill and asks that the Library measure the ruin rather than open it, since whatever lies under the stone is neither hers to claim nor his.

title: Làrach an Teampaill measured
body: The library's diggers measure the ruin called Làrach an Teampaill in the east and do not dig it, at the asking of the Seann Spioradan houses of the district. The keeper enters it as measured and let be.

title: The diggers' camp opens at Làrach an Dùin
body: Four diggers under a foreman named Cailean cut trenches through the spring above the headland at Làrach an Dùin, following the line of a coursed wall sunk deeper than any footing they have found the bottom of.

title: Ailean Leabhar rides to the trenches
body: The keeper of the Library goes down himself to Làrach an Dùin on the diggers' word that the wall they have found is older than any ruin the Library holds a record of, and spends four days at the trench's edge with a lamp and a notebook.

title: The finds laid in the Library
body: Ailean Leabhar carries the season's three findings, the wall's short entry, the measure of Làrach an Teampaill, and the copied obelisk, into the Library's own presses himself, filing the not-knowing of each as carefully as a certainty.

title: Ailean measures the temple with a chain, not a spade
body: Ailean Leabhar spends two days at Làrach an Teampaill setting down the line of the fallen wall and the fall of the ground with a chain and a level, and enters the ruin as measured, and let be.

title: Una copies the obelisk stroke by stroke
body: Una, a scribe trained under Ailean Leabhar in copying the Library's most damaged leaves, spends three weeks of fair days at the foot of the obelisk near Cnoc bheag setting down every stroke of its unread script exactly as the stone gives it, worn gap for worn gap.

title: The council pays for a fence at the obelisk
body: On the keeper's word that a stone unread for longer than the kingdom's whole span deserves at least a fence against the cattle, the council finds the money for four posts and a rail set well back from the obelisk's foot.

title: The obelisk at Cnoc bheag copied
body: A scribe of the library copies the writing on the obelisk near Cnoc bheag, stroke by stroke. It is like no script known on the island. The copy is filed and the obelisk fenced.

title: The keeper of Baile chrom's lighthouse reports the vigil
body: A Dia-thìrich keeper new to the lighthouse at Baile chrom reports the Grey Night sect's yearly vigil kept silent in the tower's own shadow, and makes no move against it, having no order that names a silent watch on open ground his business.

title: A lighthouse on the Tuathaich coast
body: The Dia-thìreach keeper of Taigh-solais Baile chrom reports to the council that the Grey Night sect keeps its vigil in the dark of the lighthouse's own shadow. The council does nothing.

title: Salt-pans of Àth bheag
body: Salt-pans are dug on the flats below Àth bheag on the east coast, and within a few years the town supplies the whole eastern seaboard. The salt goes inland by the old drove road past Baile ìseal.

title: The council answers the keeper's report with nothing
body: No order reaches the keeper of Baile chrom's lighthouse, and no word reaches the magistrate who had once fined the vigil in the open, and Ailean Leabhar enters the council's silence into the Library's register as plainly as any finding.

title: Mòrag nic Coinnich made Ailean's deputy
body: On the road home from Àth bheag, Ailean Leabhar asks Mòrag nic Coinnich to stand as the Library's deputy after a season that has taught him one keeper alone is a Library one bad season from having nobody who can speak for it; she agrees, on the condition that the register always name her deputy and never keeper.

title: Cathair fhada's grain-store
body: Cathair fhada on the southern plain builds a Crown grain-store great enough to feed the south for a season. It is filled from the south's own harvests, and first opened in the dry years at Achadh shean.

title: The grain-store at Cathair fhada opens its doors
body: In the dry weeks of a poor season the keeper of the new Crown grain-store walks out to the road and tells the first cart that passes that the south will eat that year whatever the sky withholds, and word of the opened doors outruns, by an evening, word of how bad the year will prove.

title: The second census after the Severance
body: The second census measures for the first time how far the Tuathaich live below the Dia-thìrich; until now it was only seen. The report is not made public.

title: Walter Hale dies
body: Walter Hale, first speaker of the Moot, dies at Caol mhòr. The Moot chooses Mary Coyle, a fisherman's widow, to follow him, the first woman to hold the chair.

title: The second census rides the shire roads
body: Clerks sent out a second time from Cathair dhearg tally hearth against hearth as before, but with a new column set beside the first, a figure for what a Dia-thìreach household holds and one for what its Tuathach neighbour holds, so that the count for once measures the gap rather than only setting the numbers side by side.

title: The council locks the second census away
body: The sums the shire clerks carry back to Cathair dhearg go onto a stack in the council's own keeping-room and no further; no proclamation, no minute copied to the Library, no word to any shire clerk who might have carried it on, and the twelve who asked for the count give out only that the figures want study before they want airing.

title: Walter Hale settles a carter's toll dispute
body: Keeping the thirty-year habit of hearing the furthest-travelled petitioner before the day's set business, Walter Hale hears out a carter from beyond Àth fhada over a wrongly charged toll and settles it in the carter's favour himself, his voice unhurried though the sitting leaves him more spent than harder business had the winter before.

title: Walter Hale dies at Caol mhòr
body: Walter Hale, first speaker of the Moot, dies in his own bed at Caol mhòr on the twenty-eighth of an Gearran, seventy-six years old, David beside him and Alice sent for but not in time; the Moot's business stops three days without a vote taken to stop it.

title: The north walks to Hale's burial
body: Fishermen, carters and shepherds from every part of the north crowd the roads into Caol mhòr for Walter Hale's burial, more feet on the road that week than the fair itself drew the autumn before, and he is laid in sight of the Moot's own house where he sat thirty-one years.

title: The Moot names Mary Coyle speaker
body: On the fourth day after Hale's burial the Moot sets aside a factor's son and a shire clerk both spoken for the chair and names Mary Coyle, a fisherman's widow of Caol mhòr, the first woman to hold it, by a count nobody in the room troubles to call close.

title: David Hale keeps the books under Mary Coyle
body: David Hale, who kept his father's minute-books through the years of the first fair, sets Mary Coyle's seal at her own place beside the one his father's hand had set to thirty-one years of letters, and stays on at her asking to keep the rough book as he always has.

title: Seonag nic Ille-Mhoire asks to see the report
body: Seonag nic Ille-Mhoire, who rode her own shire's tally in for the second census, asks a council clerk at Cathair dhearg to let her see the island's whole sum, on the ground that she carried the figures herself and has a right to know their total.

title: Seonag writes the refusal into her own book
body: Refused the report with no reason beyond the plain fact of the refusal, Seonag nic Ille-Mhoire writes the asking and the answer that same evening into a private book she keeps for herself and shows to no one, for a record's own sake rather than any purpose she could name.

title: Ruth Ashby and Clara Tulloch begin under Eachann mac Rath
body: Two women of the shunting country north of Caol mhòr, Ruth Ashby and Clara Tulloch, come to the surgery of Eachann mac Rath at Àth àrsaidh, who takes them without his guild's leave to be taught by watching him set bones and mix poultices through a hard, fever-crowded season.

title: The guild's men find Eachann's surgery out
body: Word from a factor's wife reaches the physicians' guild that Eachann mac Rath's two new pupils handle a lancet as steady as he does, and two of the guild's own men ride to Àth àrsaidh and watch Ruth Ashby set a child's wrist unwatched before they leave without a word to either woman.

title: Eachann mac Rath struck from the physicians' guild
body: The guild strikes Eachann mac Rath from its rolls before an Cèitean is out, its letter naming no fault in his physic, only that he taught outside its leave and to hands its charter does not recognise, and he sets the letter aside and keeps his surgery open all the same.

title: The masons sign the grain-store's mortar
body: When the last course goes onto the Crown's grain-store at Cathair fhada in the dry season, two winters building and one summer roofing, the masons sign their names in the mortar.

title: The census clerks' private note
body: Seonag nic Ille-Mhoire, one of the census clerks, leaves among her papers a note that she asked to see the report on the gap and was refused. The note came to the library with her papers after her death. It is the only mention of the report outside the council.

title: The Tuathaich doctors
body: The Moot pays for two Tuathaich women to be taught medicine by a Dia-thìreach physician at Àth àrsaidh, who takes them against the will of his guild. He is struck from its rolls. They practise in the north for forty years.

title: The Abhainn ìseal takes three bridges and the embankment
body: Three days of hard rain in am Màrt bring the Abhainn ìseal over its lower banks, and the flood carries away three bridges and a long stretch of the coal line's embankment, a carter losing his cart on the middle span but no soul drowned along that reach.

title: The Abhainn ìseal floods
body: The Abhainn ìseal, longest river of the island, breaks its banks along its lower reach and carries away three bridges and a stretch of the coal line's embankment. The line is shut most of a year, and the ports live on stored coal.

title: The coal line shuts and the ports live on stored coal
body: With a mile of embankment gone under the Abhainn ìseal's flood the coal line shuts for want of ground to run on, and the ports that lived on what it carried, Ros dhomhain and the western harbours among them, turn to whatever coal they had laid by against a leaner week rather than a whole season.

title: Mary Coyle gives her first order as speaker
body: Not yet a month in the chair, Mary Coyle calls the Moot together the evening word of the washed embankment reaches Caol mhòr and orders every northern harbour that answers to the Moot to open its own coal store and share it out by the count of hearths rather than by whoever reaches the yard first, until the line can be walked and mended.

title: David Hale keeps no second copy
body: On the night Mary Coyle gives her first order as speaker, David Hale writes it into the rough book under her name and, for the first time in two years, keeps no second copy of the day's minute by his own hearth.

title: The Hawk houses' own custodian
body: The Hawk houses of Siorrachd Cnoc bheag name a custodian of their own, Raonaid nic Iain, and seat her at Inis ìseal. The high custodian at Seann Skell will not own her. The houses carry on as if he had.

title: The Hawk houses gather at Inis ìseal to name a custodian
body: Witnesses of every Hawk house in Siorrachd Cnoc bheag crowd the hall at Inis ìseal and name Raonaid nic Iain custodian by a standing vote, each house setting meal, wool or honey on the altar's step before the hall breaks.

title: Murchadh Ruadh gives Raonaid the kept feather
body: Murchadh Ruadh of Baile fhraoich sets a white feather kept three generations in his own house into Raonaid nic Iain's hand at her naming, and she wears it pinned at her collar from that day.

title: The Hawk houses speak of a hawk for the shire's arms
body: Witnesses leaving Raonaid nic Iain's naming say openly that Siorrachd Cnoc bheag's white billet, the roll's mark for two ages, ought to be struck for a hawk, though no house yet carries the saying south.

title: Seann Skell's letter refusing Raonaid reaches Inis ìseal
body: A three-line letter from the high custodian's house at Seann Skell in the south reaches Inis ìseal, naming no fault in Raonaid nic Iain but saying the Rite's own order of worship knows no office of a Hawk custodian and so cannot own her.

title: The Hawk houses carry on as if the custodian had been owned
body: The Hawk houses fold the southern letter away unanswered and keep bringing their vigils and disputes to Raonaid nic Iain exactly as before, burying and marrying their own under no rite but hers.

title: Raonaid nic Iain at Inis ìseal
body: Raonaid nic Iain, custodian of the Hawk houses, writes out the Hawk's order of worship, which until now was spoken and never written. The Hawk houses read it aloud once a year and keep the written copy locked away.

title: Raonaid begins setting the Hawk's order into a farm account-book
body: Raonaid nic Iain starts writing the Hawk's spoken order of worship, till then carried only in a custodian's memory, into a farmer's account-book, sounding each line against the altar to match her own mother's mother's telling of it.

title: The order finished and locked in the altar's oil-box
body: Raonaid nic Iain finishes the written order at the turn of the year, reads it aloud once to the gathered houses, ties it with a strip of white feather and locks it into the iron box that once held the altar's lamp-oil.

title: A hawk for Siorrachd Cnoc bheag
body: The Hawk houses of Siorrachd Cnoc bheag ask the council to set a hawk on the shire's arms in place of the white billet the roll gave it. The council grants it, and the maor's seal is recut with a white hawk among its twelve crescents. It is the first change made to the roll at the asking of an order.

title: A delegation from Inis ìseal asks the council for a hawk on the shire's seal
body: Five witnesses from the Hawk houses, Raonaid nic Iain among them, ride to Cathair dhearg to ask the council that Siorrachd Cnoc bheag's white billet be struck and a hawk set on the shire's arms in its place.

title: The maor breaks the old die and presses the new seal
body: The maor of Siorrachd Cnoc bheag breaks the shire's old die before its assembled clerks and presses the recut seal, a white hawk among twelve crescents, into wax for the first time.

title: Six dead at the Còmhrag
body: Six fighters die at the Còmhrag, the most in any year yet. The custodians of the Rite petition for its ending. The fair-wardens of Ceann leathan, whose town lives off the crowds, refuse.

title: Six die at that year's Còmhrag
body: Six fighters, the most in any year yet, die on the trampled ground at Ceann leathan before that year's Còmhrag is called, one of them a boy of Baile ghlas not yet twenty.

title: The custodians' petition against the Còmhrag is refused
body: The custodians of the southern Rite petition the fair-wardens of Ceann leathan in writing to end the Còmhrag after six deaths; the wardens read it and refuse within the hour, on the ground the town lives off the melee's crowds.

title: The circus at Ceann leathan
body: In the year of the six dead An Siorcas Siubhail Do-thuigsinn pitches at Ceann leathan and plays to the crowds who stay on after the melee. It is said the fair-wardens paid it to come.

title: The circus pitches at Ceann leathan after the six burials
body: An Siorcas Siubhail Do-thuigsinn pitches its tents on the melee's own trampled ground within a week of the six burials, and it is said, though never proved, that the fair-wardens paid it to come.

title: The coal line reaches Ceann leathan
body: The railway is carried through to the port of Ceann leathan, so that coal may be shipped from a second harbour. The quays of Ceann leathan are rebuilt for coal-ships, and the town outgrows its walls.

title: The first coal-ship loads by lamplight at Ceann leathan
body: The first coal-ship out of Ceann leathan's rebuilt quays loads by lamplight on a winter tide, the harbour clerk noting only the hour, the tonnage and the shore gang's complaint of the cold.

title: Ros bheag's shipyard
body: Ros bheag on the west coast opens a yard for coal-ships, and the western ports need no longer send to Ros dhomhain for hulls. The shipwrights of Ros dhomhain protest to the guild court and lose.

title: Ros dhomhain's masters lose their protest at the guild court
body: The eldest masters of Ros dhomhain carry their protest against Ros bheag's new coal-ship yard to the guild court at Cathair dhearg and lose it in a single sitting, the court ruling a guild's charter binds no yard to a monopoly of the coast.

title: Ceann leathan's quays outrun its walls
body: Within two winters of the coal line's coming the quays of Ceann leathan spread half a mile beyond the old gate with no wall following them, so that a stranger riding in from the coast road can no longer say where the town begins.

title: Raonaid holds the new seal
body: Raonaid nic Iain holds the recut seal of Siorrachd Cnoc bheag in her own hands the day it reaches Inis ìseal, the hawk's wing cut spread rather than folded, and says nothing for a while that any witness troubles to write down.

title: Iain Mapa proves the deep gallery
body: Sent to measure a new shaft cut on a guild captain's thirty-year hunch, Iain mac Ruairidh finds the silver at Muileann chiar running richer with depth rather than thinner, the ore darker and heavier the further the gallery goes. He checks the figures three times before he writes them fair.

title: The silver at depth
body: The silver seam at Muileann chiar, which the Dia-thìrich kept in their own hands through the humans' time, is found richer at depth than any had looked for.
