The town's old silver guild takes a charter under the restored custom. Iain Mapa, working there since the Board sent him, measures the new faces.

title: The eastern blank-houses
body: More silver comes up from Muileann chiar than the mint at Cathair dhearg can refine. The Crown gives the villages of the eastern hills the refining of the guild's bar, with the gold washed from the stream below Baile dhìreach, into blanks for the realm-coin. The mint strikes them. The villages are paid by weight.

title: Dùn thais in the west
body: Dùn thais on the west coast is granted a court of the sea of its own, to judge salvage and wreck along its shore. At its first sitting it awards a raider's hulk to the fishermen who drove it aground.

title: The guild masters read the survey entire
body: Iain carries the deep gallery's figures to the guild hall himself and unrolls them before three masters who argue over the timbering a new shaft will need. He tells them plainly it will hold only if timbered as he has drawn it, and not an inch cheaper.

title: The silver guild of Muileann chiar chartered anew
body: On the strength of the deep gallery's yield the council renews under the restored custom the charter the humans' own Administration had let stand and then let lapse, binding the guild's captains to the Crown's tithe on every bar struck and giving the guild the courts' weight behind its bindings.

title: Gold found in the stream below Baile dhìreach
body: A village smith washing his pan of an evening finds fine gold in the gravel of the stream that turns his forge's own wheel, and tells a maor's clerk the plain truth when the coin he has put by draws the clerk's question rather than invent a lie he would have to keep.

title: The first blanks struck for the mint
body: More silver comes up from Muileann chiar than the mint at Cathair dhearg can refine, and the council gives the eastern hill villages the refining of the guild's bar, with the gold washed below Baile dhìreach, into blanks for the realm-coin, paid by weight; the first blanks go north in am Faoilleach.

title: Dùn thais in the east
body: The other Dùn thais, in the east, seat of its own shire, builds a covered market for the hill farms. For ten years the royal record confuses the courts of the two towns, until Tormod Pinn marks them west and east.

title: Siorrachd Doire chaol
body: Doire chaol, the village laid out south of the capital for the families of the royal household, has grown too great for the maor of Baile chiar to govern from his seat. The council cuts it out as a shire of its own, the only shire made since the drawing.

title: Iain Mapa marries Mòr nic Dhòmhnaill
body: Iain marries Mòr, a refiner's daughter of Muileann chiar who first proved his own scale a hair off true in front of three of the guild's captains. They are married at the guild hall in am Faoilleach, her father giving her hand and the guild's captains standing witness in place of Iain's own western kin.

title: Dùn thais in the west granted a sea court
body: The western Dùn thais is granted a court of the sea to judge salvage and wreck along its shore, after a wrecked hulk driven ashore proves too rich a prize for custom alone to divide. The court's first sitting, held on the strand, awards the wreck whole to the crews who drove it aground.

title: Dùn thais in the east opens its covered market
body: The eastern Dùn thais raises a covered market at its own shire's charge for the hill farms that had traded in its square uncovered since the town was walled, its first trading held under a roof that smells more of new-cut wood than of the produce it shelters.

title: The royal record confuses the two Dùn thais
body: A clerk at Cathair dhearg files the western court's petition and the eastern market's petition against the one town's name, both signed only "Dùn thais", and a second clerk's hand-correction holds only until the next season's post brings the same confusion again.

title: Baile chiar's maor petitions to cut out Doire chaol
body: The maor of Baile chiar writes plainly that Doire chaol, grown from a scattering of household-clerks' houses into a town proper, has outgrown a seat five miles distant, and asks that it be given a maor of its own rather than go on being governed badly at second hand.

title: Siorrachd Doire chaol cut from Baile chiar
body: The council grants the petition before the summer is old, the only shire cut new from an older one since the original drawing, Doire chaol entered onto the roll with its own arms, its own dues, and a maor of its own choosing.

title: The Baile chiar maor glad of the lightening
body: The maor of Baile chiar, reading the grant that cuts Siorrachd Doire chaol from his shire, tells his clerk he is glad of the lightening, and sends the new shire's first dues south the same season with a note wishing its maor better luck of it than he had had.

title: The dead and not dead of Doire uaine
body: Herders near Doire uaine will not graze the hills above the town, where old writings tell of a thing that is dead and does not rest. A shepherd is lost there. The magistrate enters wolves.

title: The fall at Muileann dhearg
body: A gallery of the reopened Cill ghlas district gives way under Muileann dhearg, along a line the surveyors had marked as sound. Thirty-one hewers die. It is small beside the Rending. It is the same fault.

title: Iain Mapa rides through the night to Muileann dhearg
body: Word of the fall reaches Muileann chiar by a rider sent without urgency, and Iain Mapa, two seasons into the silver works and no longer reckoned a mine matter by the Board, rides the thirty miles through the night rather than wait for morning, and goes down on the second rope with a lamp and a level.

title: Iain Mapa lays his own old maps against the new fault
body: With maps sent up from the silver guild's own store, older and truer than anything the Board keeps at Cathair mhòr, Iain Mapa finds the broken ground under the fallen gallery runs exactly where the Rending's own line ran three ages before, marked by an older hand with a single word: left, let be.

title: The thirty-one are buried in a single ground
body: The dead of the fall are buried at the edge of Muileann dhearg's own burying-yard, thirty-one graves broken in two days by every man in the town not needed underground, the district's custodian reading over each grave in turn at the families' own asking, and Iain Mapa standing the whole of it with his hat in his hand.

title: Iain Mapa writes a letter naming the fault, and does not send it
body: At his own table at Muileann chiar, Iain Mapa writes to the Board naming the fault at Cill ghlas by its true line and setting it beside the survey the Board filed and never circulated three years before; he reads it through twice, folds it, and puts it unsealed in the drawer that holds his old receipt.

title: The rules of the shafts
body: After this lesser echo of the old fall of Scàineadh Cill ghlas, new rules for digging are made. They are for Dia-thìrich workers. In the workings where Tuathaich labour they are kept loosely, and by intent.

title: The timber at Àth leathan
body: At the pits about Àth leathan, where Dia-thìrich overseers work Tuathaich hands, the new rules of timbering are posted and not paid for. The overseers' books, which came later to the library, show the timber ordered and never delivered.

title: A shepherd lost above Doire uaine
body: A shepherd new to the country puts his flock to the one shoulder of hill the town's shepherds will not graze, where the old writings tell of the Marbh-bheò, and does not come down. His dog returns alone; the town finds only his crook, driven upright into the turf.

title: The magistrate enters wolves at Doire uaine
body: The magistrate writes wolves as the cause in the shire's own book, a finding no shepherd argues and none believes, since no wolf has been seen on that hill in living memory. He tells the shepherd's mother the book wanted a cause it could hold.

title: Iain Mapa keeps a second copy of the guild's charter
body: Iain writes the silver guild's new charter into his own private book beside the receipt he carried from the Sloc Mòr and the deep gallery's own figures, telling Mòr at last that the Board never once told him his first survey of the thinning vein had proved true.

title: Mary Coyle writes to the Board naming Àth leathan's undelivered timber
body: Reading a copy of the Board's new digging rules brought north by a carter, Mary Coyle writes in the Moot's own hand asking that the rules be kept in fact at the western pits as well as in the posting, and names Àth leathan and the ordered timber that never left the yard at Ceann mhòr.

title: The Board answers the Moot in three lines and files the matter
body: The Board thanks the Moot for its concern and states that Àth leathan's timber has been referred to the district overseer for his report; no report is ever filed, and Mary Coyle's letter is kept, unanswered further, in the press at Cathair mhòr where papers go that the Board has no further use for.

title: The new digging rules sent first to Iain Mapa
body: The Board's new rules for digging after the fall are sent first to Iain Mapa at Muileann dhearg as the man who closed the district, and he finds nothing in them he would change; they are made for Dia-thìrich workers.

title: Ailean Leabhar is found dead at his own desk
body: On the third day of an t-Sultain, Mòrag nic Coinnich finds Ailean Leabhar at his desk at Muileann chaol, the harvest returns for Siorrachd Doire chaol open under his hand and his pen laid down beside them rather than dropped, so that he seems, she says after, to have finished the line he was writing before he stopped.

title: Mòrag nic Coinnich, keeper
body: Ailean Leabhar dies at Muileann chaol, and Mòrag nic Coinnich becomes keeper of the library. She begins the custom, kept ever since, of writing beside each item whence it came.

title: Ailean Leabhar is buried in the ground behind the Library
body: Ailean Leabhar is buried two days after at Muileann chaol, in a small ground behind the Library itself where no keeper had been buried before him, the town turning out near to the last household, and Mòrag nic Coinnich reads over him only his own words, that the Library settles nothing and only keeps.

title: Mòrag nic Coinnich finds an unfinished note among Ailean Leabhar's papers
body: Going through the old keeper's desk in her first month as keeper, Mòrag nic Coinnich finds one sheet in his own hand, undated beyond an old year, reading only that what the Library is not sent it cannot keep, and to ask the shires again; she cannot say whether it was a note to himself or the start of a letter, and keeps it unfiled in her own drawer.

title: The pit families of Achadh dhomhain
body: After the fall at Muileann dhearg forty hewers' families leave Achadh dhomhain for the fishing ports of the south. The Guild of Hewers binds sixty apprentices to fill its rolls. None of them are Tuathaich.

title: Sixty apprentices are bound at Achadh dhomhain, and not one is Tuathaich
body: The Guild of Hewers binds sixty boys in its own hall at Achadh dhomhain to fill the rolls the fall thinned by thirty-one, each swearing with a hand laid on a lump of coal while his father stands behind him in a line the length of the hall, and the charter that reserves the oath to Dia-thìreach applicants is kept to the letter.

title: A family with no dead in the fall leaves Achadh dhomhain regardless
body: Among the forty households that quit Achadh dhomhain for the southern ports that autumn are families who buried no one in the fall, saying to whoever asks that a town may grieve its thirty-one and go on living beside their graves, but a household does not choose to raise its own sons under ground a survey has already misjudged once.

title: Fire at the fair
body: On the eve of Samhain fire runs through the stalls of the fair at Muileann òg. The next day the fair's court sits in a field, and the fair goes on. Oighrig nic Mhathain, toll-mistress since the first fair, dies of her burns.

title: Oighrig nic Mhathain is burned beating back the fire with her own cloak
body: Caught in the fairground when the fire runs on Samhain eve, Oighrig nic Mhathain beats at the burning canvas with her own cloak until the worst of it is turned from the stalls that hold a dozen towns' whole trade, and does not leave the ground until the last flame along the weavers' row has burned itself out.

title: The Tuathaich wool carts
body: The Rail Board will not carry goods sent by the Moot, pleading the fair's rule on factors. The wool of the north goes south to Muileann òg by cart, five days on the road, and is sold by factors when it comes.

title: Mary Coyle asks the Board whether its reading of the factor rule is new
body: When the Rail Board refuses to carry the north's wool on the strength of the fair's own rule on factors, Mary Coyle writes a second, shorter letter asking only whether the reading is new or has simply never before been turned against the north's own goods; the Board does not answer it, and a clerk files it beside the first.

title: Forty households entered 'gone south'
body: The tally-clerk of Achadh dhomhain enters the forty households leaving for the southern ports off the town's roll with two words against each, gone south, the roll keeping no other word for it.

title: Oighrig nic Mhathain dies of her burns
body: Oighrig nic Mhathain presides over the court of the fair from a chair carried into the burnt field, her hands bound in linen, keeps the fair open to its appointed end, and dies of her burns at her own house at Muileann òg before the month is out, fifty years old.

title: The new toll-mistress sells the north's wool through the factors
body: The new toll-mistress at Muileann òg, keeping the fair's rules as Oighrig left them, sells the north's cart-borne wool through the factors when it comes, and enters the sale in the fair's book under the makers' shire.

title: The Tuathaich carters' road
body: The carters of the northern wool go to the fair by Cnoc ghorm, Àth fhada and the old road down to Inis àrsaidh, and the Tuathaich villages on the way open inns for them. In the north the road is called the Carters' Road. In the south it has no name.

title: Daniel Frayne rides the wool carts south
body: With the Rail Board still refusing the Moot's goods, the north's wool goes south by cart, and Daniel Frayne asks leave to ride with the second train, five days on the old way by Cnoc ghorm, Àth fhada and Inis àrsaidh to the fair at Muileann òg.

title: Dubhan's childhood
body: Dubhan grows up watching a caste that does not age hold every true advantage on an island where his own forebears were pushed to the edge. The coal was never his to inherit.

title: The Moot's pit register
body: The Moot at Caol mhòr begins a register of Tuathaich hewers killed or maimed in the western pits, for no Dia-thìreach book counts them. Mary Coyle's clerks enter the first year's names on the families' own word. The register is kept to this day and has never been sent south.

title: The first lamp lit at Àth fhada
body: A widow of Àth fhada who has fed carters at her own table for two winters begins taking payment for it, keeping a lamp lit past every other house's hour. Two more households on the road do the same within the season, and carters find their beds by the lights alone.

title: The north's name and the south's silence
body: Frayne asks the widow at Àth fhada what the carters call their road and learns it has long been called the Carters' Road in the north, its name simply grown to fit the wool's going by cart. He learns too that no map south of Cnoc ghorm troubles to name the road at all, and writes both facts down.

title: A season's wages weighed against the road
body: Waiting out a flood at a crossing short of Inis àrsaidh, Frayne hears from a shunting family how the road's five days are reckoned against a season's whole earning, a toll no southern ledger is ever asked to set against the fair's own profit. He writes the figure down.

title: Mary Coyle opens the register of the hurt
body: Mary Coyle tells the Moot's clerks that the Board keeps no true count of the Tuathaich dead and maimed of the western pits, and that the Moot will begin a book naming them on the families' own word, since no other word will be offered.

title: The first name entered in Clàr nan Leòn
body: The widow of Àth fhada's husband, lost under the western pits, is the first name Daniel Frayne writes into the new register, carried south by a neighbour rather than wait on the widow's own journey. Frayne sets the pen down before the ink is dry.

title: The keel laid at Ros mhòr
body: Shipwrights turned out of the southern guild yards gather enough coin and timber at last to lay a keel of their own at Ros mhòr. Harry Marlow, grey now, cuts it to the humans' old lines, low and full in the bow, that the southern guilds no longer let a Tuathaich hand build.

title: The wool train waits out the flood
body: The second wool train of the winter sits a night at the flooded crossing short of Inis àrsaidh and goes on when the water drops, losing half a day to the weather and none of the wool, its lead carter holding that a road worn long enough finds its own way round a flood.

title: Ros mhòr's boatyard
body: Tuathaich boatbuilders turned out of the guild yards open a boatyard at Ros mhòr in the north. Its boats are built to the humans' old lines and are swifter than anything in the south.

title: Tormod Pinn
body: Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill lays down the office of royal chronicler. Tormod mac Sheumais follows her, called Tormod Pinn for the speed of his hand. He keeps the record for more than twenty years and writes more of it than any before or since.

title: A second copy of the register kept apart
body: By the year's end the register holds above thirty names. A second copy is made against fire or flood and kept at a house in Muileann leathan, so that no single hand's slipping can lose the names a second time.

title: Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill's last entry
body: Feeling her hand begin to shake on a long day's writing, Gormshuil lays down the office of royal chronicler after four and twenty years, her final entry a plain list of what the chronicle under her hand had never held: the northern towns' own accounts, the humans' old treaties, and the Board's surveys left unrolled.

title: Tormod Pinn copies the list of gaps
body: Tormod mac Sheumais, called Tormod Pinn for the speed of his hand, succeeds Gormshuil as royal chronicler and opens his own first book by copying her last list whole, striking nothing from it, so it is not lost to be rewritten by a less patient hand.

title: The first Ros mhòr hull launched
body: Built on evenings and Sabbaths through a year, the yard's first hull takes the water clean at Ros mhòr, swifter than anything the southern yards have launched in a long season. Harry Marlow tells the men beside him he means to live to see the north sail hulls built with no southern guild's leave.

title: Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill's last entry
body: Tormod Pinn copies into the front of his first book the last entry Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill made as chronicler, a list of what the record lacks: the northern towns' own accounts, the humans' treaties in their own tongue, and the Board's surveys. He adds nothing to it.

title: Tormod Pinn adds his own line to the list of gaps
body: Riding the southern circuit his predecessor once rode, Tormod Pinn adds beneath Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill's list of what the chronicle lacks a line of his own, that a gap named is worth more than a gap forgotten, and copies both into the chest that goes to the Library.

title: Dry years at Achadh shean
body: Dry years come again to the country about Achadh shean, where the Long Drought settled in the humans' time. This time the council sends grain up the coal line and pays for it out of the Sloc Mòr's share. No one in the shire dies of hunger, and the chronicler records it.

title: The maor of Achadh shean petitions early
body: With three wells of the drove road gone brackish and a fourth dry to the stone, the maor of Siorrachd Achadh shean writes south before the second month of the dry is out rather than wait for the harvest itself to fail, and asks that a man argues with a poor harvest but a well gone to stone argues with no one.

title: The wells of Siorrachd Achadh shean
body: The maor of Siorrachd Achadh shean has twelve wells dug to the rock along the drove road, each marked with the name of the shire and of the council. Water is drawn from four of them still.

title: A fifth well dug dry on a dowser's word
body: Of the twelve wells the maor of Achadh shean has cut along the drove road, one stands dry from the day it is dug, sited on a dowser's hazel rather than any surveyor's word, and the well-diggers own the fact afterward without much shame in the owning.

title: Grain by the coal line
body: The grain for Achadh shean comes from the store at Cathair fhada, and for the first time it goes by the coal line. The Rail Board charges the council for the carriage.

title: The first wagons reach Achadh shean in the rain
body: The Cathair fhada store's grain reaches the sidings at Achadh shean by the coal line on the morning the season's first proper rain falls at last, and the maor, standing in the mud he had prayed six weeks for, tells the carters the grain waited on the roof to prove it was not wanted.

title: Raiders at Baile ìseal
body: Raiders land near Baile ìseal on the far east coast and burn the salt-sheds of Àth bheag. The kingdom's patrol boats come two days later and find the sheds cold.

title: The salt-sheds of Àth bheag rebuilt
body: The burned salt-sheds of Àth bheag are raised again within the year, the Crown paying a third of the cost as it once paid a third of Cuan dhearg's relief, and the salt trade limps through the interval on what the barrels spared from the fire can carry.

title: The patrol captain's report on the two days
body: Called to answer before the shire's maor, the patrol's captain writes a report naming the distance, the wind and the hour the alarm reached his harbour; the Board judges it honest, and the households of Àth bheag, hearing it read at the market cross, judge it an accounting that answers every question but the one that matters.

title: Murchadh mac Coinnich's log
body: Murchadh mac Coinnich, keeper of Taigh-solais Baile ìseal, begins to enter in the lighthouse log every unlit ship he sees, with her heading and the hour. His logs, kept most of his life, are the fullest record of the eastern raiders in the library.

title: The Board's inspector calls the Baile ìseal log the emptiest on the round
body: The Lighthouse Board's own inspector, checking oil against entries at Taigh-solais Baile ìseal, tells Murchadh mac Coinnich that his log is the tidiest on the eastern round and the emptiest, a remark Murchadh takes for a compliment until he comes, within the year, to hear it differently.

title: Murchadh buys a second book at his own coin
body: Murchadh mac Coinnich buys, from a Muileann leathan binder a carter brings up the coast, a book of his own beside the Board's, in which he means to set down what the Board's own log has no line for: every ship that crosses under his light showing no lamp.

title: Murchadh among the ash at Àth bheag
body: Once relief has come for his light, Murchadh mac Coinnich rides down to Àth bheag the second morning after the burning and stands with the ford-keepers among the wet ash and the barrel-hoops of the salt-sheds, hearing from a woman of the trade what the fire has cost.

title: The pirates' names
body: The raiders fly no flag, and Murchadh mac Coinnich's log names their ships as the fishermen of Àth bheag name them. From his log the names pass into the royal record.

title: The salt-carrier names the raiders' hulls
body: An old salt-carrier at the Àth bheag quay gives Murchadh mac Coinnich the coast's own names for two dark hulls that have crossed under his light unlit, An Ròn Dubh for her low black run and An Fhaoileag for a habit of standing off by day and closing only with the dark.

title: Murchadh's book copied fair for the royal chronicle
body: A Library clerk carries Murchadh mac Coinnich's private log south, and Tormod Pinn draws the names An Ròn Dubh and An Fhaoileag into the royal record from it, crediting no better source than a keeper's own ledger and the salt-carriers of a coast the patrol once answered two days late.

title: The Còmhrag at its height
body: The Còmhrag draws its greatest crowd yet to Ceann leathan, and the fair-wardens build timber stands along three sides of the field. The champion is Ealasaid nic Coinnich of Àth ghlas, the first woman to win it. She does not fight again.

title: Ealasaid nic Coinnich declines to defend the year's honour
body: Asked by the fair-wardens whether she will defend the champion's honour the following year, Ealasaid nic Coinnich tells them a thing won once stays won whether or not she stands the field a second year, and returns to her family's trade at Àth ghlas.

title: Murchadh's first full year of the unlit ships
body: By the second an Dùbhlachd of his own keeping, Murchadh mac Coinnich's private book holds above thirty crossings, most nameless still, ruled by a straight-edge and set on the shelf beside the Board's own log as the truer account of what sails the eastern water dark.

title: The Hawk river port of Cnoc bheag
body: Cnoc bheag, greatest town of the Hawk country, passes Cathair mhòr in its numbers. Its river quays take the grain of the north-central country, and its Hawk house is the richest of any order outside the capital.

title: Scoiltean nan Draoidhean revived
body: The druid schools of Flidais, silent since the humans ruled, open again. Their first question, why the vein answers some and not others, presses hard once more, for the vein itself is failing.

title: Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain's lectures
body: The first teacher of the revived school is Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain. She lectures in the sacred wood of Flidais near Muileann chiar in the east, where the druids last met under the humans, and opens with the school's oldest question, plainly put: why the vein answers some hands and not others.

title: The old druid houses mended before the teaching
body: Before a single lecture is given, villagers near Muileann chiar mend the doors and sills of the long-shut druid house with green timber and their own hands, asking no wage beyond a bench kept for them once the teaching begins.

title: An old cutter's son questions Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain
body: After her first lecture in the sacred wood, an old man whose father kept the Holy Age strike-books asks Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain whether she means to answer her own question before she finishes teaching it. She tells him plainly that she does not.

title: The druid schools in Siorrachd Baile gharbh
body: The houses of the druid schools in Siorrachd Baile gharbh in the north-east, silent since the humans' time, open again at Baile gharbh and Àth fhada. Their teachers walk to the sacred wood to hear Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain, and walk back.

title: The school at Caol shean
body: The druid school takes a house at Caol shean, one of the great druid towns of the east, and teaches there in the wet months, when the wood is too sodden for lectures. Its students copy the census note on the coal-touched and dispute it openly.

title: The Hawk given a place
body: A council of the Rite at Seann Skell offers the Hawk houses of Cnoc bheag a place under the high custodian with their own order of worship. The Hawk houses take the place and keep their order. After this the quarrel is quieter. It does not end.

title: The Baile gharbh teachers' first walk south
body: Teachers of the reopened druid houses in Siorrachd Baile gharbh walk the better part of a week to hear Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain teach in the sacred wood before daring to open the question in their own halls, and do not miss a winter's walk after.

title: The census line argued by lamplight at Caol shean
body: In the wet-house at Caol shean a miller's son newly come to the school asks why the census line for the coal-touched should be a matter no one may question, when the vein itself is questioned daily under the same roof; the argument runs past the hour the hearth is banked.

title: The Muileann dhearg hall given back to the school
body: The Guild of Hewers' captains give the school the hall at Muileann dhearg, shut since a gallery there closed three years before, on the one condition that nothing taught in it name a living captain or gallery; the school keeps to it gladly.

title: The Hawk's terms read a seventh time
body: At a council of the Rite at Seann Skell on the southern coast, the high custodian's clerks read the Hawk houses of Cnoc bheag the same settlement offered six times before; this time no witness raises the old objection, and the terms stand.

title: A Baile gharbh teacher's minute of the walk
body: The youngest of the Baile gharbh teachers, a woman not yet twenty on her first walk south to the sacred wood, writes of the journey in her school's own minute-book, and her school does not miss a winter's walk after.

title: The north-eastern harbours
body: Caol chrom and Caol gharbh on the north-east coast join their harbour dues to pay for a breakwater across the strait between them. It is eight years in the building and is the longest on the island yet.

title: Daniel Frayne's copying school
body: At Muileann leathan in the north Daniel Frayne, a clerk of the Moot, teaches young Tuathaich to copy and bind books, since the guilds of that craft in the south will not take them. The bindings of Muileann leathan are found afterwards in Dia-thìrich libraries without their makers' names.

title: The Abhainn uaine ferries
body: The boat-landing at Cidhe Beag on the Abhainn uaine is licensed as a ferry, to carry passengers and small freight down the river toward the coast. The first to hold the licence is an old boatman who had worked the landing without one for forty years.

title: Daniel Frayne opens his bindery at Muileann leathan
body: Daniel Frayne builds a press from a mended cider-press and teaches young Tuathaich hands to fold, sew and board a book, a craft the southern guilds have never let a Tuathaich learn under their own mark; he asks no guild's leave to teach it.

title: Frayne's first bindings sold south without his name
body: The bindery's first plain-calf volumes, carrying no maker's name, are carried south with the wool carts and sold to Dia-thìreach households who praise the binding's neatness to Frayne's own face, none of them knowing whose pupils' hands had actually sewn the spine they hold.

title: The first stone of the Caol chrom breakwater
body: Caol chrom and its neighbour across the strait lay the first stone of a shared breakwater, the longest yet built on the island, meant to close a strait that has drowned more boats in a hard winter than either shire's harbour dues could bear alone.

title: The old boatman's licence at Cidhe Beag
body: The boatman who has rowed the crossing at Cidhe Beag on the Abhainn uaine for forty years without leave asked or given is granted a licence at last by the shire's maor, more for the shire's own records than for any change in how he rows or reckons his fare.

title: Tormod Pinn marks the two Dùn thais west and east
body: Finding the Crown's returns beginning to run its two towns of one name together, Tormod Pinn rules a fresh line across the royal record marking Dùn thais in the west against Dùn thais in the east, and sends word to both shires' clerks to take more care.

title: Loch chrom
body: The fishermen of Loch chrom, the only great lake of the island, are licensed to net its trout, which was kept for the Crown's table. Each year the Crown's table is served first.

title: The pillar at Cnoc chiar
body: Students of the druid schools try to read the pillar near Cnoc chiar by setting it beside the obelisk at Cnoc bheag and the column at Cnoc ghorm. They find signs in common and no meaning. Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain writes that the Old Ones were here and said so, and that none living can hear it.

title: Three slates carried to Caol shean
body: Three of Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain's students ride from the sacred wood to copy the pillar near Cnoc chiar, the obelisk over Cnoc bheag's quays and the column at Cnoc ghorm onto separate slates, and carry them back through the rain to lay side by side.

title: A mark in common on three stones
body: Comparing the three copied slates by lamplight, the students of Caol shean find a mark like a bent reed and a straight double stroke cut on all three stones and nowhere else known to them, and no meaning in either that any among them can bring out.

title: Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain writes the Old Ones' sentence
body: Reading the three slates laid together at Caol shean, Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain writes that the Old Ones were here and said so, and that none living can hear what they said; her students copy the sentence into every school's minute-book after her.

title: Flood at Inis chrom
body: A storm tide floods the lower town of Inis chrom on the south-west coast and drowns the net-lofts and the rope-walk. The town builds both again on piles, and so they stand now.

title: Inis chrom's lofts rebuilt on piles
body: After the storm tide drowns its net-lofts and rope-walk, Inis chrom does not ask the Crown for its rebuilding. Its own carpenters raise both a second time on driven piles a fathom above the old floor, timber floated down the Abhainn ghorm from the woods above Àth gharbh, the work finished before the autumn herring.

title: Cnoc leathan's schools
body: Cnoc leathan in the east opens a school in every one of its six parishes, paid from the shire's dues, the first shire to do so. The council asks how it paid for them and is shown the accounts.

title: Cnoc leathan's sixth parish school
body: The last and smallest of Cnoc leathan's six new parish schools opens with eleven children on its benches and a teacher hired from Baile chiar. The council's clerk, sent to ask how the shire paid for six schools at once, is shown plain accounts and asks nothing further.

title: Alasdair mac Ùisdein's loan
body: Alasdair mac Ùisdein, grandson of the first holder of the Sloc Mòr concession, borrows against his house's share to pay for a search for a second vein. The Mine Board lends its surveyors. The Crown lends its name.

title: Catrìona nic Neacail lent to the search
body: The Mine Board names eleven surveyors to Alasdair mac Ùisdein's search for a second vein. Catrìona nic Neacail, thirty-two, a chain-hand risen through the vein-towns, is one of them, and tells a senior surveyor riding out with her that she would rather walk ground and find nothing than be told years on that nobody looked.

title: The druid school on the search
body: Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain writes to the Mine Board that the search asks the wrong question. The school has always asked why the vein answers some hands, she says, and no one has asked why there is one vein. The Board files the letter.

title: Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain's letter read a second time
body: A Board clerk sorting the year's correspondence finds Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain's letter on the search, filed unread when it was first sent, and carries it to Catrìona nic Neacail along with Mòrag nic Coinnich's. Catrìona keeps a copy of both beside her own last entry, though she judges the school's question and the Board's chain answer to different masters.

title: The search for a second vein
body: The search for a second seam of the coloured coal elsewhere on the island is costly, and finds nothing. The same search had been made in the Age of Ailean, thousands of years before, and had failed in the same way; it had been forgotten.

title: The first shaft above Dùn dhearg
body: The search's first shaft goes down above Dùn dhearg in stone that gives every hopeful sign, the diggers wagering small coin among themselves on the day the vein will show. It is judged barren within the fortnight, the first entry in a tally that will run to forty-one.

title: Forty-one dry shafts
body: The borings of the search run from the hills above Dùn dhearg to the moors south of Baile ruadh. Forty-one shafts are sunk, and none strikes the vein. Afterwards Mòrag nic Coinnich finds in a list of the Holy Age at the library the same hills named as searched and barren.

title: The moor's own name, am Fearann Falamh
body: An old digger of Dùn dhearg tells Catrìona nic Neacail the moor's shepherds have long called the search's ground am Fearann Falamh, the empty ground, meaning only that no shepherd ever found a spring there worth the digging. The name outlasts the search's own hope of it.

title: The forty-first shaft struck dry
body: The last shaft of the search, sunk on the moor south of Baile ruadh through the hardest weather any of the forty had asked, strikes water at a depth no vein has ever answered. Catrìona nic Neacail writes the word barren in her own field-book a forty-first time and sits a while on the spoil-heap before riding to report it.

title: Mòrag nic Coinnich finds the Holy Age roll
body: Cataloguing the Library's lower room, Mòrag nic Coinnich finds a Holy Age survey naming the same hills above Dùn dhearg and moors south of Baile ruadh, searched once and found barren ages before, the surveyors' own names worn from the roll. She sends Catrìona nic Neacail word the same week the forty-first shaft is closed.

title: The Library's copy of the old survey promised south
body: Catrìona nic Neacail copies Mòrag nic Coinnich's letter into her own field-book beside her last entry and resolves to see the Holy Age roll sent south in copy, so that any surveyor sent to the same ground again will not have to wait on a keeper's own cataloguing to learn what the last search cost.

title: Sheep fall into the open shafts
body: On the moor south of Baile ruadh, where the ground is softest and the covering poorest, sheep begin falling into the search's open shaft-mouths before the first winter is out, three that the shire's reckoning can put a number to and likely more that no reckoning counts.

title: Dùn dhearg's claim
body: The town of Dùn dhearg, whose hills held a dozen of the dry shafts, claims damages from the house of Mac Ùisdein for spoiled grazing. The circuit court awards them. The house pays a third before it sells.

title: Dùn dhearg's shepherds testify at the circuit court
body: At the circuit court's hearing of Dùn dhearg's claim, two shepherds swear that grazing spoiled by the search's spoil-heaps is lost longer than any digger reckoned, one saying he lost more lambs to the search's own open ground in two years than to wolves in ten. The court finds for the town.

title: The house of Mac Ùisdein sells half
body: To meet its debts the house of Mac Ùisdein sells half its share in the Sloc Mòr back to the Crown. Its stone house at Cathair mhòr is let to the Mine Board, which moves its offices there.

title: The Mac Ùisdein stone house let to the Board
body: Its coin thinned by the search and Dùn dhearg's damages, the house of Mac Ùisdein lets its stone house at Cathair mhòr, kept in the family since the first holder's day, to the Mine Board, which moves its offices into it the following spring.

title: The shafts at Baile ruadh left open
body: The dry shafts of the search are left open on the moors near Baile ruadh. Sheep fall into them, and one child, before the shire fences them at its own cost. The shire's claim on the house of Mac Ùisdein for the fencing is never paid.

title: The child of Baile ruadh lost to an open shaft
body: A child of Baile ruadh, out after a stray lamb on ground she has walked without harm a hundred times, falls into one of the search's uncovered shafts and is not found until the day after. The parish's own book holds her name and the day, and nothing more.

title: Baile ruadh votes to fence the forty-one shafts
body: The shire of Baile ruadh votes to fence every one of the search's forty-one shafts at its own cost rather than wait on the Crown, and enters a claim against the house of Mac Ùisdein for the fencing's cost that is never paid. The fencing goes up through the summer, post and wire round every covered mouth.

title: A mother takes the long road at Baile ruadh
body: The mother of the child lost in the open shaft at Baile ruadh will not walk that road again the whole of the year after, and takes the longer way round by the mill whatever the weather asks of her.

title: The Muileann dhomhain mills
body: The mills of Muileann dhomhain in the south-east ground grain for the vein-towns. When the vein-towns' orders fall they turn to grinding bark for the tanners. The miller-families of the town keep their mark and change their trade.

title: Muileann dhomhain's mills turn to bark
body: With the vein-towns' grain orders thinned by scarce coin, the mills of Muileann dhomhain begin grinding bark for the coast's tanners instead of grain. The miller-families keep the mark cut into their stone before any shire held a charter to license it, and change the trade under it without asking the Board's leave.

title: A Muileann dhomhain miller answers a Board clerk
body: Asked by a passing clerk whether it troubles her to grind bark at a wheel her family has ground grain at for four generations, the eldest of the Muileann dhomhain millers answers that a wheel does not know what is under it, and the grain will come back once the vein-towns have coin to buy it with again.

title: The rope-makers of Seann Tarr
body: The rope-makers of Seann Tarr on the north-east coast are chartered as a guild, the last guild the restored custom makes for a trade the humans had not touched. Their hemp comes from the fields about Doire uaine and Achadh naomh.

title: The rope-makers of Seann Tarr chartered
body: The restored custom charters the rope-walks of Seann Tarr as a guild, the last trade the humans never touched to be given a charter of its own. Its hemp is carted down from the fields about Doire uaine and Achadh naomh by roads older than the survey lines that have tried more than once to straighten them.

title: Seann Tarr's chest remembered
body: By the shire's own rule the rope-makers' charter at Seann Tarr is kept in the shire's chest and not sent to Cathair dhearg. The shire keeper of Seann Tarr keeps a list of what the chest holds and sends the list alone.

title: Seann Tarr's chest sends only its list
body: Asked to send the new rope-makers' charter south to the Board's own files, the shire keeper of Seann Tarr answers that the charter will stay in the shire's own chest, and sends a rider south with a list of what the chest holds and no more. No second rider is sent to ask again.

title: The Circus at Inis àrsaidh
body: An Siorcas Siubhail Do-thuigsinn is recorded again, pitched this time on the common near Inis àrsaidh in the west. The magistrate who licenses it enters the acts as 'various' and the fee as paid.

title: The circus at Inis àrsaidh licensed as 'various'
body: An Siorcas Siubhail Do-thuigsinn pitches again on the common near Inis àrsaidh. The magistrate who licenses its acts, unable to put a name to half of what he has watched, enters the whole of it in his book as various and the fee as paid, an entry the Library's copyists find hardest of the year to gloss.

title: A list is cheaper to lose than a charter
body: It is said at Seann Tarr, not without pride, that a shire which will not send its papers south need never trouble over what is done with them there, and that a list is a cheaper thing to lose than a charter.

title: Ceann mhin's fish-market
body: Ceann mhin, the great port south-east of the capital, opens a covered fish-market over the old strand. Fish from Seann Bhral and the eastern grounds is sold there for the capital.

title: Ceann mhin roofs its fish-market
body: Ceann mhin opens a covered market over its old strand for fish carried up from Seann Bhral and the eastern grounds, the first roof the port has raised over the trade. The strand's old traders grumble at first, and grumble less once a wet winter lets them keep a fire by the scales.

title: Edged tools banned from the Còmhrag
body: A fighter is killed with a hewer's pick, and the fair-wardens of Ceann leathan ban edged tools from the Còmhrag. Staves and fists are still allowed, and so the deaths go on, fewer.

title: Edged iron banned from the Còmhrag
body: After a fighter is killed at Ceann leathan with a hewer's pick carried in under a borrowed coat, the fair-wardens ban edged iron from the ring. Staves and fists are still allowed, and the dying goes on, slower, which a warden of long standing calls the whole of what the ban was ever meant to promise.

title: The drowned lighthouse keeper
body: The keeper of Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg on the south coast drowns going out to a boat aground on the reef below the light. The boat's crew are saved by his daughter, Ciorstaidh nic Artair, and she is given the keeper's warrant in his place.

title: Artair mac Mhurchaidh drowns off Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg
body: When a Doire shean fishing boat strikes the reef below the light in a hard south-west wind, keeper Artair mac Mhurchaidh, fifty-three, goes out alone with a rope and brings two of the four crew ashore, then goes back for the other two and does not return the third time, after above thirty years keeping that light.

title: Ciorstaidh nic Artair brings in the last of the crew
body: Waking to find her father's boat gone, Ciorstaidh nic Artair, three-and-twenty, takes the second boat out along his own rope's line and finds the wreck, her father's rope still fast to it. She rows the last two of the Doire shean crew ashore herself, a boat built for a lighter woman than she then is.

title: Artair mac Mhurchaidh buried above the light
body: Artair mac Mhurchaidh's body comes ashore three days after the wreck and is carried back to Tobar dhearg, to the ground above the light where every keeper before him lies. The parish register enters against his name the day, the manner, and the single word every drowning of that water is given: drowned.

title: The Board confirms Ciorstaidh nic Artair's warrant
body: Asked by the shire's own maor whether the daughter of a keeper who died bringing in four lives with two boats and one rope may keep the light he kept, the Board at Cathair dhearg writes back within the month that she may, and enters the warrant in her name without recorded debate.

title: Ciorstaidh nic Artair's reef mark
body: Ciorstaidh nic Artair has an iron post set on the reef below Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg, painted and hung with a bell. While she keeps the light no boat goes aground there.

title: The reef post raised by subscription
body: Ciorstaidh nic Artair has an iron post sunk into the reef at low water, painted the red of danger marked and known, and hung with a bell cast at Muileann chiar. Half the cost comes from the Board's purse and half from a purse the fishing families of Doire shean and Tobar dhearg make up between them.

title: The Board's engineer approves the reef bell
body: The Board's engineer walks the reef at low water and pronounces the post sound and the casting good. Asked whether she means to add clockwork to strike the hour as well as the danger, Ciorstaidh nic Artair answers that a man wanting the hour has a tide table and two eyes, and needs neither bell nor clockwork for that.

title: Mary Coyle lays down the chair
body: Mary Coyle lays down the chair of the Moot at Caol mhòr. Daniel Frayne of Muileann leathan follows her, the first speaker born after the Severance.

title: The reef bell first rings in fog
body: In a fog thick enough to hide the light itself, the bell on its post rings of its own weight as the sea moves it, and every boat working that stretch of coast steers home by the sound alone. No boat goes aground on the reef below Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg that year, nor in any year Ciorstaidh nic Artair keeps the light after.

title: Mary Coyle lays down the chair of the Moot
body: After two-and-twenty years in the chair, Mary Coyle lays it down at Caol mhòr, speaking of the register of the western pits' dead and maimed her hand began and the coal line her petitions never once moved south of Àth leathan, and names before the Moot rises the man she asks it to choose after her.

title: Daniel Frayne chosen speaker of the Moot
body: Daniel Frayne of Muileann leathan, who bound books for the north's schools when the southern guilds would not take a Tuathaich name, is chosen speaker without a voice raised against him: the first to have been born after the Severance closed, and Mary Coyle's own right hand in the chair for above ten years before it.

title: The Fèill's northern day
body: The court of the fair at Muileann òg sets aside one day of the fair for goods from the northern shires. They are still sold through Dia-thìrich factors, but under the northern makers' own marks. It is the first time a Tuathaich name is written on anything sold there.

title: Two Seann Vell masons set the reef post
body: Two masons brought up from Seann Vell drive and cement Ciorstaidh nic Artair's iron post into the reef below Taigh-solais Tobar dhearg, working only the hour either side of the ebb for the better part of a month.

title: The grey twill first on the pole
body: Daniel Frayne, six months in the Moot's chair, watches the first cloth of the fair's northern day go up on its pole at Muileann òg: a grey twill of Doire ghlas dyed with the shire's own bark, with a single white thread at the selvedge.

title: The Tuathaich marks at the fair
body: The first northern mark sold under its own name at the fair is the cloth of the weavers of Doire ghlas, a grey twill with a white thread at the selvedge. The southern weavers of Baile chiar begin to weave a white thread into their own.

title: The Doire ghlas weaver's daughter sews by lantern
body: At the fair's close on its first northern day, a Doire ghlas weaver's daughter left minding her mother's stall sews a second white thread into an unsold bolt after the buyers have gone. Asked why she troubles with it unwatched, she says the mark goes in whether anyone buys it or not, since a thread sewn only for show is no mark at all.

title: Baile chiar's weavers name their own thread pale
body: Rather than claim the white thread already spoken for, the weavers of Baile chiar work a grey scarcely darker than the wool into the selvedge of their own finer bolts. An old weaver tells Daniel Frayne, who asks why the south troubles to copy a northern habit, that she has woven forty years without her name on a bolt and does not mean to die without it.

title: The Depletion laid bare
body: The quiet note of the survey in SE 26 is now an open trouble. The last unworked stretches of the vein are found, and they are smaller than any wish to own.

title: Catrìona nic Neacail begins the one sheet
body: Catrìona nic Neacail, a Board surveyor sixteen years standing, begins drawing every stretch of the true vein still unopened onto a single leaf, working outward through the Board's own scattered rolls a shire at a time and riding to settle every ground the rolls disagree on.

title: Catrìona nic Neacail's map
body: Catrìona nic Neacail, surveyor-general of the Mine Board, publishes the map of the vein's last unworked stretches. It fits on one sheet. Within the year she gives up her post and goes to teach at the druid school at Caol shean.

title: A concession-holder asks the sheet a plain question
body: A concession-holder of four generations' standing stands before the finished sheet the better part of an hour, then asks Catrìona nic Neacail plainly whether the red marked over his own family's ground means ten years or thirty, having daughters to settle and no wish to be told later that the Board had always known and never troubled to colour it in.

title: Catrìona nic Neacail named surveyor-general
body: The Board names Catrìona nic Neacail surveyor-general, an office left empty three years for want of anyone troubling to ask what it was for, until her one-sheet map of the vein's last unworked stretches made plain that somebody ought to answer for the whole of what it showed. She is the youngest to hold it in living memory.

title: Duilleag na Fèithe hung on the chamber wall
body: Catrìona nic Neacail publishes Duilleag na Fèithe in an Dùbhlachd in the plainest way the Board knows, hanging it on the wall of its own chamber at Cathair mhòr, where every surveyor, clerk and concession-holder who comes can stand before it.

title: Iain Mapa's survey found
body: Among the Board's files Catrìona nic Neacail finds Iain Mapa's survey of thirty years before, which shows the same thinning she has just measured. She sends a copy to the library, with a note of when the Board received it.

title: Two surveys read side by side
body: Catrìona nic Neacail sits late at the Board's own table beneath her own sheet, reading her map and Iain Mapa's thirty-year-old survey side by side by lamplight, the same failing ground marked out in the same terms three decades apart, and cannot say which survey troubles her more, the one that found the truth or the one believed too late to matter.

title: Catrìona nic Neacail's visit to Muileann chiar
body: Catrìona nic Neacail rides east to Muileann chiar and sits with Iain mac Ruairidh, three-and-sixty and failing, in what proves his last spring. He shows her his own copy of his old survey with the Board's receipt still pinned to it, and asks whether the school at Caol shean still keeps its old question about the vein.

title: Iain Mapa dies
body: Iain mac Ruairidh, called Iain Mapa, dies at Muileann chiar, where the Board sent him. His own copy of his survey is found among his papers with the Board's receipt pinned to it.

title: Iain Mapa buried by the silver guild
body: The silver guild of Muileann chiar, which had paid Iain mac Ruairidh's small pension ten years, buries him with an ounce of its own refined silver laid beside him, its master saying over him that he had gone into more of the mountain's dark than any three men living and had never once come up lying about what he found there.

title: Mòr nic Dhòmhnaill sends her husband's papers south
body: Going through her husband's papers, Mòr nic Dhòmhnaill finds the folded survey with the Board's old receipt still pinned to it and sends the whole of it to the Library at Muileann chaol, writing only that he had asked more than once it not be lost a second time, and that she knew no safer place to send it.

title: Muileann dhearg empties
body: In a few years Muileann dhearg loses a third of its households to the ports. Its druid hall is shut, and its bell sold to the school at Caol shean, where it rings for lectures still.

title: Muileann dhearg's maor counts the empty houses
body: Muileann dhearg's maor keeps a count of houses left empty as families leave for the ports and the southern yards, a tally kept at first from ordinary habit and then from something nearer alarm, running within three years to above sixty within the shire's own walls.

title: The Fèidh hall's last teacher locks its door
body: The last teacher of Muileann dhearg's Fèidh hall, given back to the druid school not ten years before, locks its door herself for want of a congregation left to keep it and carries the key to the maor's own house rather than leave it with no one.

title: Ceann leathan's coal quays idle
body: Coal-ships wait at Ceann leathan for cargoes that come in half-loads. The harbour dues fall by half, and the fair-wardens raise the gate-price of the Còmhrag to make it up.

title: Ruairidh the cellar boy
body: A clerk's boy of twelve who has fetched bundles in the Board's own cellar at Cathair mhòr for three years tells Catrìona nic Neacail she is the first to ask him to read a label aloud rather than simply hand a bundle across. He helps her keep the tally of the week's search among the old presses.

title: Catrìona nic Neacail resigns the surveyor-general's office
body: Within the year of finding Iain Mapa's old survey, Catrìona nic Neacail resigns as surveyor-general, the Board's own minute recording it in four flat lines, and asks a place teaching at the druid school at Caol shean, judging the mountain's own answers now the only lesson in her trade worth the passing on.

title: Ceann leathan raises the Còmhrag's gate-price
body: With the harbour dues at Ceann leathan fallen by half as coal-ships wait for cargoes that come in half loaded, the fair-wardens, whose town lives as much off the coal trade as off the yearly melee, raise the gate-price of the Còmhrag to make up what the quay no longer earns.

title: The Muileann dhearg bell rings Catrìona's first lecture
body: Catrìona nic Neacail gives her first lecture at Caol shean in the same wood where Seonaid nic Ghill-Eathain once first put the old question to her students, and the bell taken down from Muileann dhearg's shut hall, hung now in the school's own tower, is rung for the first time to call the school in.

title: Iain Mapa dies at his workbench
body: Iain mac Ruairidh dies at his own workbench at Muileann chiar in the first days of an Cèitean, not a fortnight after Catrìona nic Neacail's visit; Mòr finds him in the evening with small objects laid out before him in an order only he had understood.

title: Baile Mòr dhomhain's market
body: As the trade of the coal-towns falls away, Baile Mòr dhomhain in the northern hills becomes the market for the wool and hides of the hill country. For two years together its market day draws more carts than the fair at Muileann òg.

title: Daniel Frayne notes the gaps at Muileann òg
body: A wool-buyer at the Moot's own table tells Daniel Frayne that the fair at Muileann òg now stands with gaps between its tents where none stood before, the fair's own wardens filling them each year with a wider aisle rather than own that the crowd has thinned.

title: Mairead crowned
body: Eòghan's reign ends in the decade that the Depletion becomes known to all. Mairead inherits a kingdom whose founding wealth is plainly failing, for the first time since the restoration.

title: The old die broken at Cathair dhearg
body: With Mairead crowned, the die that struck Eòghan's own likeness on the realm-coin is broken at Cathair dhearg by the mint's custom, the old coin kept good until the new is struck in number enough to answer for it.

title: The Hewers bind no apprentices
body: For the first time since its charter the Guild of Hewers binds no new apprentices. Its masters vote to keep the rolls open to the sons and daughters of members only.

title: Agnes Pike dies
body: Agnes Pike, who opened the byre school at Doire ghlas in the fifteenth year, dies at seven-and-seventy; Daniel Frayne, reading Muileann shean's letter for primers that season, remembers her telling him that a trade a man carries in his own head weighs nothing on the road.

title: Muileann shean's school of hewers
body: Muileann shean in the north opens a school for the sons and daughters of hewers who will not be bound, and teaches them to read, reckon and survey. Most of its first pupils go to the ports.

title: Daniel Frayne binds primers for Muileann shean
body: Asked for primers by Muileann shean's own maor, Daniel Frayne binds forty copies of a reading-book at his own bench at Muileann leathan and sends them north on the first cart with room, the forms unchanged since he first set the type twenty years before.

title: Muileann shean's benches pass thirty
body: The school Muileann shean opened for hewers' children the Guild will not bind grows within the year from eleven pupils to above thirty, though three of the first eleven have already gone south to hire themselves out as chain-hands in the ports.

title: The Doire ghlas mills
body: Wool mills are built at Doire ghlas with the Moot's money, the first works in the north that owe nothing to the vein. The Rail Board refuses their cloth, until a ruling of the circuit court at Seann Bhral compels it to carry any goods that pay the rate.

title: The first bolt off the Doire ghlas looms
body: The wool mills raised at Doire ghlas with the Moot's own coin turn their first bolt, a grey twill with a white thread at the selvedge, and the overseer writes to Caol mhòr that it is better cloth than the south's own factors reckoned a northern loom could turn out.

title: The Rail Board refuses the first wagon
body: The Rail Board's factors at Àth leathan, the railhead nearest the north, refuse to carry the Doire ghlas mill's first wagon-load south to Muileann òg, giving no reason beyond the Board's own long custom of judging for itself what the line will carry.

title: The Moot brings its suit to Seann Bhral
body: Daniel Frayne rides west to the circuit court at Seann Bhral with the mill's ledgers and the Board's letter of refusal, asking Ruairidh mac Phàdraig to rule whether a carrier chartered by the Crown may refuse one people's cargo and take another's.

title: The Seann Bhral ruling
body: Ruairidh mac Phàdraig, circuit justice at Seann Bhral, rules that the Rail Board is a carrier of the Crown and must carry for any who pay. It is the first ruling the Moot wins in a Dia-thìreach court. The Board appeals, and the council lets the appeal lapse.

title: The charter read clause by clause at Seann Bhral
body: When the Rail Board's factor argues at Seann Bhral that the Board's rails answer to a different clause of its charter than its carts, Ruairidh mac Phàdraig has the whole charter read aloud clause by clause, and no clause is found that names the rails apart.

title: The Crown's share of the Sloc Mòr
body: The Crown buys the last working shafts of the house of Mac Ùisdein at the Sloc Mòr and leaves the house its share in the spoil and the quarry. Thenceforth the Board works the vein in the Crown's name alone.

title: Word of Catrìona nic Neacail's going
body: A Board clerk's notice of the Mac Ùisdein sale reaches Caol mhòr with a passing word that the surveyor who drew the search's last sheet has resigned her post to teach at Caol shean, a name Daniel Frayne knows only at second hand.

title: The copper at Àth fhiadhaich
body: Copper is found in the hills behind Àth fhiadhaich in the eastern hills. The Board opens a working with men laid off from the Sloc Mòr. It pays wages. It is not the vein, and the town's Seann Spioradan house gives it no blessing.

title: The first Doire ghlas bale rides the coal line
body: A year after the ruling, the Rail Board's own factor at Àth leathan weighs the first Doire ghlas bale onto the wagon without comment, the same weight given any cargo that pays the rate, and Daniel Frayne rides down to see it loaded.

title: The council lets the Board's appeal lapse
body: The Rail Board's appeal against the Seann Bhral ruling lies on the council's table a winter and a spring and is let lapse in the summer, the council's minute noting only that the matter was not reached in the session's business.

title: Mary Coyle dies at Caol mhòr
body: Mary Coyle, speaker of the Moot from the thirty-third year to the fifty-fifth, dies at Caol mhòr in the second week of an t-Iuchar at nine-and-seventy, having asked that nothing be read over her but the names.

title: Mary Coyle buried near Walter Hale
body: Mary Coyle is laid in Walter Hale's ground, a little lower on the slope within sight of the Moot's house, and the priest reads over her only the eleven drowned of Cuan bheag, the widows of the bench by the door and her own name; three Ros mhòr men who sailed with her to Seann Bhral bring the tiller of her boat.

title: Mary Coyle's sheet kept in the Moot's chest
body: The Moot votes without a count that the sheet of the eleven drowned and the widows after them, given it by Mary Coyle's family, be kept in its own chest beside the register of the hurt with the space beneath the last name left empty; no notice of her death goes south.

title: Àth fhiadhaich's copper-town
body: The copper workings at Àth fhiadhaich draw miners from the failing vein-towns. The town builds a new street for them and names it for the Sloc Mòr, and the Seann Spioradan house there speaks against the name.

title: The street named for the Sloc Mòr
body: Miners settled on Àth fhiadhaich's new street carry small lumps of coal from the Sloc Mòr's own upper galleries among their goods, keeping them for the plain fact of the carrying rather than for any use, while the Old Spirits' keeper tells the council a street named for another town's mountain risks forgetting the ground it stands on.

title: Dubhan begins his experiments
body: Dubhan makes his first attempts to draw a fuel to stand in the coal's place from the waste of the mines. They fail, and little is set down of them.

title: Dubhan's first working set down
body: Tormod Pinn enters a single sentence in the day-book on a report from the north, that a young man there has made trials at drawing a fuel from the waste of the mines and that they have come to nothing; he writes no more of it.

title: The Sloc Mòr's pumps
body: The lowest galleries of the Sloc Mòr are let flood, for the pumps cost more to run than the coal beneath is worth. The Board's minute calls it a pause.

title: The last pump drawn out
body: Tormod Pinn rides to Achadh dhomhain and finds the Sloc Mòr's lowest galleries eleven fathoms under water, the pumps cold on the Board's own order; the overseer there has kept the order's own slip folded in his coat since the turn of the season, as though he expected someday to need to prove it.

title: The first pump goes down the coal line
body: The first of the Sloc Mòr's three great pumps goes south under canvas on a flat wagon from a siding above Achadh dhomhain, bound for the new dry dock at Seann Bhral in the south; Tormod Pinn watches it pass and sets down that a pump goes where the water is and cares no more for the ground it served than a bolt of cloth.

title: The pumps sold
body: The Board sells the great pumps of the Sloc Mòr to the harbour at Seann Bhral in the south, where they drain the new dry dock. In the next generation they are the only engines of the vein still at work.

title: The third pump follows and six men are found other work
body: The overseer at Achadh dhomhain writes that the third and last pump has gone to Seann Bhral in the south after the second, and that the six men who tended the three between them have been found work on the galleries still above water, a thing the Board's own notice calls no loss to any household.

title: The maor of Baile dhomhain writes of the crossing
body: A shire's maor writes to the Board of stock lost along Imrich nam Pantar near Baile dhomhain, a loss too large for wolves and weather; the Board's clerk, having no ledger fit to hold it, sends the letter on to the Library.

title: The panthers cross the south-west
body: A great host of panthers crosses the south-west near Baile dhomhain. For a month the herders lose stock. Tormod Pinn writes it down as a thing named in the lists of the Holy Age and not seen in living memory.

title: The old list of An Aois Naomh opened again
body: Tormod Pinn sets the maor's letter beside a Library list from the days of An Aois Naomh naming the years the panthers crossed before, an interval longer than any living herder's working life, and writes the crossing's entry longer than any other that year.

title: The herders keep the crossing days
body: The herders of the south-west drive their flocks off the old road beforehand and keep the crossing as a season of watching, losing fewer beasts in the end than the first week's count had feared, though more than an ordinary year costs them.

title: The hides of Baile ghorm
body: Tanners at Baile ghorm on the south-west coast buy the hides of the panthers the herders kill, and their trade outlasts the crossing by ten years. Saddles of panther-skin from Baile ghorm are sold at the fair at Muileann òg under the town's mark.

title: Baile ghorm's tanners buy the hides
body: Buyers from Baile ghorm ride up into the hills within the fortnight to take the hides of panthers the herders' dogs and spears have brought down, paying a price the herders judge fair for a skin they have no other use for.

title: Panther-skins first at the fair
body: The fair at Muileann òg sees, for the first time in any chronicler's memory, saddles and belts of panther-hide sold under the Baile ghorm mark, the southern buyers taken by surprise enough that the mark's own price doubles twice before the fair is out.

title: Imrich nam Pantar in the chronicle
body: Tormod Pinn's entry on the panthers is the longest in his book for that year. He sets it beside the list of the Holy Age, and notes that the old list names the year after the panthers as a hungry one.

title: Muileann mhin halves its lamp-making
body: The lamp-makers of Muileann mhin halve their making for want of coal to fire their forges properly, the coal reaching the town thinner and dearer each season the Sloc Mòr's galleries give less of it up.

title: The Sloc Mòr's pumps drain the dock at Seann Bhral
body: The three great pumps of the Sloc Mòr, set on a bed of masonry at the head of the new dry dock at Seann Bhral in the south, pump it dry for the first time on the ninth day after the third is fired.

title: A coal-ship first stands in the Seann Bhral dock
body: The first hull stood dry in the new dock at Seann Bhral is a coal-ship out of Ceann leathan with her keel sprung on the bar; by the year's end eleven hulls have stood in it, and the town's shipwrights raise a shed over its head.

title: The dock's return filed under the harbour
body: Tormod Pinn enters Seann Bhral's return of the dock in the royal chronicle without a line of his own, copies into its margin the names the Achadh dhomhain men used among themselves for the three engines, and asks that the return be filed under the harbour and not under the Board.

title: The Achadh dhomhain overseer signs his name
body: The overseer at Achadh dhomhain writes to Tormod Pinn that the second pump has followed the first to Seann Bhral and the third stands ready, and that the six men who tended them have been found work on the galleries above water; he signs his own name to it this time rather than none.

title: The coal-lamp shortage
body: The lamp-makers of Muileann mhin halve their making, for want of coal to burn in the lamps they make. Shaft-lamps are lent from pit to pit, and the guild's minute-book records who lent to whom.

title: The Guild's lending-book
body: The Guild of Hewers keeps a plain minute-book at its hall for shaft-lamps lent from pit to pit, and Tormod Pinn, sending for a copy of its first year, finds more names entered against debts than against repayments, a dry column that tells the vein's own thinning more plainly than any Board letter.

title: The yard families stop the trains
body: The yard families at Muileann chrom stop the coal trains for three days over a cut wage, putting forward as their spokesman Dòmhnall Ruadh mac Ailein, one-and-forty, whose father laid the yard's first rail; a Tuathaich minister there keeps his own book of the families' grievances.

title: Unrest at Muileann chrom
body: The yard families at Muileann chrom stop the coal trains for three days over cut wages. On the fourth day the Rail Board settles; on the fifth it dismisses eleven men.

title: The Board settles and dismisses eleven
body: The Board's factor restores the old wage on the third day and the trains run again on the fourth; on the fifth the Board's own notice names eleven men dismissed for their part in the stopping, Dòmhnall Ruadh mac Ailein among them, the settlement and the dismissal arriving from the same hand in the same week.

title: Cathair fhada's granaries want a second storey
body: The maor of Cathair fhada writes to Muileann chaol that the year's harvest has proved thicker than any since before the search for a second vein was spoken of, granaries built for a lean year now wanting a second storey to hold it.

title: The hungry year that was not
body: The harvest after the panthers' crossing is good across the south. Tormod Pinn records it and strikes through his own note of the year before.

title: Tormod strikes through his own note
body: Tormod Pinn draws a line through his own entry naming a hungry year to follow the panthers' crossing, leaving the words legible beneath it and writing that the harvest proved thick rather than thin, since a chronicle owes its readers its wrong guesses as plainly as its right ones.

title: The third census after the Severance
body: For the first time in the Rìoghachd the numbers of the people are published openly. It is a small token of openness, and nothing else is changed.

title: Census clerks come north for a count
body: Two census clerks ride to Caol mhòr, the first southern office to ask the Moot for its own count of its own people rather than take none, the shire's own maor having told the surveyor-general no clerk had yet gone north.

title: The Moot's figures given to the census clerks
body: Daniel Frayne gives the visiting clerks the Moot's own count, kept every third year since the room was opened, along with the school and vigil registers, and offers to swear to the figures before a justice if the council should ask it.

title: Frayne's private book notes the asking
body: Daniel Frayne writes the day's giving into his own private book, judging it worth the keeping that the Moot had, for once, been asked for its figures rather than merely tolerated in the giving of them.

title: The figures read at the Moot
body: The published figures are read aloud at the Moot at Caol mhòr. They show the northern towns at about half the Dia-thìrich measure in every column the clerks chose to take. The Moot's minute says only: 'Now written.'

title: A young clerk asks what the two words mean
body: Walking out of the room into the frost, a junior clerk asks Daniel Frayne whether the minute's two words oblige the south to answer for what it has printed; Frayne tells him a fact set down is not a promise kept, but cannot be unprinted either.

title: The count of the touched
body: The published census, like the first, has a line for the coal-touched. It gives a number and nothing more. Tormod Pinn copies it into the chronicle without comment, as Gormshuil nic Dhùghaill did for the first.

title: The census in the Stone's shires
body: In the shires of Òrd na Cloiche in the south-west the houses of the Stone publish for the first time their own count of their people beside the kingdom's. The two agree within a hundred.

title: Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh
body: Tormod Pinn dies at his desk at Muileann chaol. Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh becomes royal chronicler. She is the first to add at the foot of each year a note of what the record could not learn.

title: Tormod Pinn buried at Muileann chaol
body: Tormod Pinn, chronicler nine-and-seventy years old, is buried in the small ground behind the Library among every keeper and chronicler the house has kept since Ailean Leabhar; Mòrag nic Coinnich speaks over him that he kept the list honest and struck nothing from it unearned.

title: Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh's first morning at the desk
body: Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh, chosen from the Library's own senior clerks, tells the house on her first morning as chronicler that she means to change nothing of the desk's hours, only its habit of silence where the record itself keeps none.

title: The Hawk houses' registers
body: The Hawk houses of Siorrachd Ros gheal send their birth-rolls to the library for the first time, on condition that they be filed under Òrd an t-Seabhaig and not under Òrd Bhrìde. Mòrag nic Coinnich agrees.

title: Tormod Pinn found at his desk
body: Tormod Pinn is found dead at his desk at Muileann chaol on a morning in an t-Sultain, the year's returns open under his hand and his pen laid down beside them; the clerks write his age, nine-and-seventy, in the margin of his last page, the only line of his tenure he did not write himself.

title: A Ros gheal carter waits in the Library's yard
body: The carter who brings the three iron-bound coffers of the Ros gheal Hawk houses' birth-rolls to Muileann chaol waits the whole of an afternoon in the Library's yard, under orders to turn his horse for home if the keeper will not file them under Òrd an t-Seabhaig.

title: Mòrag's three lines to the Hawk houses
body: Mòrag nic Coinnich answers the Hawk houses in three lines in her own hand before dusk: the rolls will be filed under Òrd an t-Seabhaig in a press of their own, the houses may send a witness to see it, and the Library will keep a copy and send it back if asked.

title: A paper filed under its sender's name
body: For the first time the Library files a paper under a name its sender sets against the name its own register gives; Mòrag nic Coinnich enters the fact plainly, and beneath it that she does not think the Library has any business teaching the Hawk houses what to call themselves.

title: Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh's first foot-note
body: Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh's first note of what the record could not learn concerns the northern shires: the census clerks were told the figures and did not count them, and the figures they were told were the Moot's.

title: Beathag's note sent north to Frayne
body: A Library clerk sends Daniel Frayne a copy of Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh's first foot-note, naming the census clerks' reliance on the Moot's own figures; Frayne keeps it in his private book beside the day he gave them, judging her a chronicler the north may trust.

title: The record-chests called in
body: Mòrag nic Coinnich's clerks go to thirty shire towns to bring their record-chests to Muileann chaol. At Seann Tarr the shire's keeper burns the chest sooner than send it, saying that the shire's record belongs in the shire. He is fined; the chest is lost.

title: Mòrag nic Coinnich calls the shire chests in
body: Mòrag nic Coinnich sends her own clerks along the roll to bring every shire's record-chest to Muileann chaol, judging a history kept in forty scattered chests no history at all but forty separate hopes of one day being read together.

title: The Seann Tarr keeper meets the clerks at the gate
body: The shire keeper who burned his own chest at Seann Tarr meets Mòrag's clerks at the gate the next morning, his coat still smelling of the smoke, and repeats to them plainly that the shire's record belongs in the shire.

title: Cathair naomh sends its rolls
body: The keeper of Cathair naomh in the north sends her shire's rolls to the library in two carts, with the town's own chronicle, kept by one family for four generations. Mòrag nic Coinnich enters it as the best-kept shire record received.

title: Cathair naomh's chronicle carried south by its own keeper
body: The eldest daughter of the family that has kept Cathair naomh's town chronicle four generations rides the two carts south herself and unpacks them at Mòrag nic Coinnich's own table, the chronicle begun by her great-grandmother on the back of an unused rent-roll.

title: A fourth coffer from Ros gheal
body: The Ros gheal carter comes south again the next spring with a fourth coffer of birth-rolls found in a shut room at the houses' oldest altar, and reports that the houses read Mòrag's three lines aloud in their hall and said nothing of them after, which in the Hawk country is how a thing is accepted.

title: The Seann Tarr keeper fined for the burning
