body: The council fines the old keeper of Seann Tarr for burning the shire's chest; he pays without argument and without apology, and whatever the chest held of the shire's two centuries is lost entire.

title: The Seann Toll chest
body: Seann Toll in the north sends its chest willingly and asks for a copy of all that is in it. Mòrag nic Coinnich's clerks make the copy, and the shire's copy is the pattern for every copy the library has made since.

title: Seann Toll's copy becomes the pattern
body: The full transcription Mòrag's clerks make for Seann Toll, bound and set beside the original before either leaves the shire's hall, becomes the pattern every later shire's copy is cut to.

title: The library enlarged
body: Leabharlann Muileann chaol doubles its holdings and takes several lesser archives of the provinces into one record. From this time the history of Dia-thìr is kept in one place and not in many.

title: Frayne puts the calling-in to the Moot's own room
body: Reading the notice of the calling-in, Daniel Frayne calls the room at Caol mhòr together and asks it plainly whether the Moot should offer its own books south now that the council has shown a wish to gather every shire's record.

title: No northern chest
body: No Tuathaich record is called in. The Moot's minute-books, the schools' registers, the churches' registers and the vigil-books of Baile chrom stay in the north, in private keeping, as they always have.

title: The Moot's minute declining to send its books
body: After an evening's debate, the room's minute at Caol mhòr records no vote by count and no reason beyond two words its clerk sets down at the close of the sitting: *kept north.* No cart of the Moot's own books goes south that year or after.

title: The library's new wing
body: The enlarged library is housed in a new wing at Muileann chaol, built of the grey stone of the Sloc Mòr's spoil. The chests of the provinces fill three floors. The fourth is left empty for what was not sent.

title: The new wing's three floors and the empty fourth
body: Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh walks the new wing at Muileann chaol before its chests are carried up, and finds three floors built to hold the provinces' returns, town chronicles and vigil-books, and a fourth, raised to the same measure, left empty for a record that has not been sent.

title: Beathag's first foot-note on the empty floor
body: Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh keeps Tormod Pinn's list at the front of the year's book unchanged and adds, beneath it, her own foot-note that the fourth floor stands ready and that no cart has come, judging the sentence plainer than any she could set beside it.

title: The tally of the calling-in read floor by floor
body: Reading the whole tally of the calling-in set out floor by floor for the first time, Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh finds that every shire the council's roll accounted for sent something, willing or not, and that the one record never asked for is the one never received.

title: The branch line to Àth leathan closed
body: The Rail Board shuts the branch line to Àth leathan, pleading the falling yield of the western pits. The Tuathaich pits go on working, and their coal goes by cart to the western ports and by boat from there.

title: The Àth leathan branch shut for falling yield
body: The Mine Board withdraws its overseers from Àth leathan along with the branch line, its own wages no longer answering for the western pits' falling yield, and the pits pass, without any charter forbidding it, into the keeping of the hewers who work them.

title: The Moot's hewers take the pits
body: The Board's overseers are withdrawn from Àth leathan, and the Tuathaich hewers there go on working the pits under their own pit captains, paying the Crown's fifth under the Leòid ruling. The Board takes the payments and enters them as arrears.

title: The Àth leathan hewers pay the fifth and are entered in arrears
body: The pit captains the Àth leathan hewers choose from their own number weigh every cart and set by the Crown's fifth under the Leòid ruling, sending word south each season; the Board takes the payments when a carrier brings them and enters them in its own books as arrears.

title: The first Àth leathan coal carted to Seann Bhral
body: The pit captains at Àth leathan send the season's first coal south by cart rather than by rail, three days slower on the road but loaded and sent on the hewers' own choosing, down to the coal factors' yards at Seann Bhral in the west.

title: Cnoc thais in the western hills
body: At Cnoc thais in the western hills the Tuathaich pits pass to their hewers when the Board's overseers leave, and the father of the pit captain Tom Varley is chosen to keep the accounts. Here the town's own register of the pits begins.

title: Sam Varley opens the pit's own book at Cnoc thais
body: When the Board's overseer leaves Cnoc thais, Sam Varley, who has kept a private tally beside the Board's own scale for eleven years, opens a book of the pit's own accounts headed only with the day and the pit's name, the earliest page the town's register still keeps.

title: Tom Varley runs the book's errands
body: Sam Varley's small son Tom, not yet old enough for the pit, carries the figures the book wants between the scale-house and his father's table; told that a book kept honest for nobody outlasts one kept honest only for someone watching, he carries them straight all the same.

title: The Sligeanach's great year
body: An Sligeanach Fad' às, the roadside tavern by Ceann bhàn on the southern road, is sold to a family of drovers from Achadh mhòr, who build a second hall for the drove trade. It becomes the greatest house on the old mining roads.

title: An Sligeanach Fad' às sold to a family of drovers
body: The family that kept An Sligeanach Fad' às three generations sells it to drovers new to the trade, who raise a second hall beside the first; within a few years it is the largest house on the old mining roads, grown fat on the drove trade as the coal roads empty.

title: The eastern fishing grounds fail
body: For the second year together the herring do not come to the grounds off the mouth of the Abhainn chaol below Seann Dunn. The east-coast boats go north to fish the grounds off Caol mhòr, which the licence law keeps for them, and the Tuathaich boats are pushed farther out.

title: The herring fail a second year off Seann Dunn
body: The herring do not return, a second season together, to the grounds off Seann Dunn, and the east-coast boats, finding their own waters empty, take to fishing the grounds off Caol mhòr that the licence law has long kept for the northern boats.

title: Inis mhin's boats
body: Pushed from their grounds by the eastern boats, the Tuathaich boats of Inis mhin fish the deep water beyond the northern isles. Two are lost in the first year and none after, and the catch of Inis mhin passes that of Caol mhòr.

title: Inis mhin's boats pass Caol mhòr's own catch
body: Pushed from their nearer grounds by the crowding of east-coast boats, the boats of Inis mhin take the deep water beyond the northern isles; two are lost the first year and none after, and before the next season is out the catch they bring in passes what Caol mhòr itself takes from the grounds the law still calls its own.

title: Raghnall mac Mhuirich, keeper
body: Mòrag nic Coinnich lays down the keepership after some thirty years. Raghnall mac Mhuirich, her deputy, becomes keeper of Leabharlann Muileann chaol.

title: Mòrag nic Coinnich lays down the keepership
body: Mòrag nic Coinnich, two-and-seventy and thirty years and more in the chair, lays down the keepership of the Library, walking the fourth floor once more with Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh and saying only that she built the room and leaves the asking to whoever holds the chair after her.

title: Raghnall mac Mhuirich made keeper
body: Raghnall mac Mhuirich, fifty that year, takes the chair Mòrag nic Coinnich lays down and changes nothing of the Library's hours or custom in his first year, a steadiness the clerks under him come to value in a season when little else about the kingdom's coal holds steady.

title: The coal price at the fair
body: The Board cuts its sales, and the price of coal-fuel at the fair at Muileann òg doubles. The fair's court fixes a ceiling price and cannot hold it.

title: The fair's ceiling set on coal and broken in every stall
body: When the Board cuts its sales and the price of coal-fuel at Muileann òg doubles, the fair's court sets a ceiling price by its long custom; within a season no factor sells at it, the coal not reaching the stalls at the named price, and the wardens do not cry the ceiling's breaking.

title: Beathag's foot-note on the capital's cold
body: Beathag nic Fhionnlaigh's foot-note for the year names what the record cannot learn: how many grates in the capital's poorer wards went unlit for want of coal, a count no census asked for and no shire kept, so that the Library holds no reckoning of its own kingdom's cold.

title: Coal thieves at Cnoc fhiadhaich
body: Households of Cnoc fhiadhaich are found picking coal from the spoil-heaps to burn, and the Board posts watchmen there. The watchmen are men of the town, and see nothing.

title: The watchmen at Cnoc fhiadhaich see nothing
body: The Board posts watchmen of the town itself over the spoil-heaps at Cnoc fhiadhaich against households picking coal to burn; every night of the posting the watchmen see nothing, though the heaps grow lower and the poorer grates burn warmer than the fair's price could otherwise buy.

title: The capital's poorer streets burn short hours
body: In the capital's poorer wards the street lamps burn shorter hours than the council's lighting order requires, the keepers no longer able to afford in full an order written for coal at half the price it now costs; the council's own notice calls the shortening a saving.
